articles.title: Global Ship Lease reports higher Q3 profit as charter backlog reaches $3.4 billion
articles.summary: Global Ship Lease (GSL) reported higher revenue and earnings for the third quarter of 2026, supported by stronger charter rates and continued demand for containership capacity. The company recorded operating revenue of $201.4 million, up 4.5% from $192.7 million in the same period of 2025. Net income available to...
articles.body: Global Ship Lease (GSL) reported higher revenue and earnings for the third quarter of 2026, supported by stronger charter rates and continued demand for containership capacity. The company recorded operating revenue of $201.4 million, up 4.5% from $192.7 million in the same period of 2025. Net income available to common shareholders increased to $99.2 million from $92.6 million, while earnings per share rose to $2.75 from $2.59. Adjusted EBITDA also increased to $138.8 million, compared with $130.2 million a year earlier. The results come as GSL continues to secure long-term employment for its fleet. At the end of September, the company had contracted revenue of $3.4 billion, including its newbuilding programme. Charter coverage extends into 2028 Global Ship Lease added approximately $1.82 billion in contracted revenue during the first nine months of 2026. This came from new charters, extensions and initial employment agreements for 15 newbuildings. As a result, the company reported charter coverage of 100% for 2026, 98% for 2027 and 74% for 2028. Its contracted revenue backlog extends over an average remaining period of 3.5 years on a TEU-weighted basis. George Youroukos, Executive Chairman of Global Ship Lease, said changing liner networks and disruptions to global shipping routes continue to support demand for flexible containership capacity. He also pointed to port congestion, extreme weather and imbalances in cargo flows as factors affecting vessel availability. Meanwhile, fleet utilisation reached 96.6% during the third quarter, compared with 95.9% a year earlier. Fleet renewal and financing programme As of 30 September 2026, Global Ship Lease operated 71 containerships and had another 17 vessels under construction, with deliveries scheduled between late 2028 and early 2030. The company previously announced the addition of two containerships to its newbuilding programme , bringing its total orderbook to 17 vessels. Fifteen of these ships have secured multi-year charters, with an average firm duration of 7.1 years on a TEU-weighted basis. The remaining two vessels are still subject to discussions regarding future employment and financing. GSL has also arranged a $1 billion syndicated financing facility for the 15 contracted newbuildings. The seven-year facility will be drawn in stages as the vessels are delivered. In addition, the company announced an increase in its quarterly supplemental dividend. The total quarterly dividend will rise to $0.6875 per common share, equivalent to $2.75 annually. For the first nine months of 2026, operating revenue increased to $598.1 million from $575.5 million. However, net income available to common shareholders declined to $279.9 million from $306.7 million. The previous year’s results included a $28.3 million gain from vessel sales, which contributed to the difference between the two periods. Global Ship Lease continues to focus on long-term charter coverage and fleet renewal as it prepares for the delivery of its next generation of containerships.

articles.body: Operations Press Releases Splash Crew launches to put seafarers at the heart of maritime news Splash November 10, 2026 0 332 2 minutes read Splash Maritime Group has unveiled Splash Crew , its latest specialist news platform, with the ambition of becoming essential daily reading for seafarers, crewing professionals, shipmanagers, regulators and maritime technology companies worldwide. The new publication builds on Splash’s longstanding commitment to championing seafarers and examining the human side of an industry responsible for moving global trade. The platform delivers international news, interviews, analysis and features covering crew welfare, recruitment, retention, training, safety, working conditions, regulation, career development and the rapidly changing technologies being introduced onboard ships. The publication will also examine some of shipping’s most pressing workforce challenges, from seafarer shortages and fatigue to mental health, connectivity, criminalisation, abandonment and the implications of automation and the energy transition for those working at sea. Splash Crew is designed to bridge the gap between life onboard and decisions made ashore, bringing together perspectives from seafarers, fleet managers, crewing agencies, training institutions, technology providers and policymakers. “At Splash, we’ve always believed that seafarers deserve far more attention than they typically receive in the maritime media,” said Sam Chambers, co-founder and editorial director of Splash Maritime Group. “Shipping is very good at telling us that people are its greatest asset, but the reality onboard does not always match the rhetoric. We want Splash Crew to examine that gap, celebrate the people who make this extraordinary industry work and challenge practices that need to change. “Crucially, this isn’t just another crew welfare publication. We want to cover every aspect of working life at sea, from the technologies arriving on the bridge and in the engine room to the changing demands placed on today’s officers and ratings. Our ambition is to make Splash Crew the first site seafarers and shipmanagers turn to every day.” The launch follows Splash’s publication of its inaugural Seafarers Report in 2025, which examined the growing importance of bringing the voices of those working onboard into corporate decision-making. Splash Crew will apply the same editorial philosophy that has underpinned Splash’s growth over more than a decade: fast, independent, informed reporting that respects readers’ time. The new platform also provides a dedicated global audience for the companies developing solutions to improve shipboard operations, training, safety and quality of life at sea. Splash Crew joins an expanding portfolio of specialist maritime publications from the Singapore-headquartered media group, including SplashTech , Splash Ports , and Splash Cruise . Visit Splash Crew at splashcrew.com . Follow Splash Crew on LinkedIn . Sign up to Splash Crew Log weekly newsletter (commencing in 2027). articles.title: G7 launches 14-port alliance to tackle global drug trafficking
articles.summary: Fourteen major ports are joining forces in a new G7-backed initiative aimed at combating drug trafficking through international shipping networks, with artificial intelligence and closer intelligence sharing central to the programme. The G7+ Ports Network was formally launched yesterday in Marseille, bringing...
articles.body: Ports and Logistics Regulatory G7 launches 14-port alliance to tackle global drug trafficking Sam Chambers November 10, 2026 0 47 1 minute read Australian Federal Police Australian Federal Police Fourteen major ports are joining forces in a new G7-backed initiative aimed at combating drug trafficking through international shipping networks, with artificial intelligence and closer intelligence sharing central to the programme. The G7+ Ports Network was formally launched yesterday in Marseille, bringing together the world’s leading industrialised economies alongside Brazil and South Korea. The initiative connects port authorities, customs organisations and law enforcement agencies in an attempt to identify suspicious container movements and disrupt the maritime routes used by organised crime. Participants include ports in Marseille, Le Havre, Dunkirk, Hamburg, Genoa, Busan and Houston. International organisations involved include Interpol, the International Maritime Organization, the World Customs Organization and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the network will use tools including artificial intelligence to track suspicious shipments and improve information exchange between ports. The initiative was first proposed at June’s G7 summit in Évian, where leaders identified maritime transport as a principal route for international trafficking in narcotics and precursor chemicals. According to Barrot, approximately 70% of illegal drugs entering France arrive through ports, highlighting the challenge of screening enormous container volumes without disrupting legitimate trade. France has signed more than 20 bilateral agreements targeting drug trafficking since late 2025 and increased specialist personnel deployed in Latin America and the Caribbean by more than 30%. The new network is intended to build on those agreements by coordinating investigations across origin, transit and destination ports. articles.body: Finance and Insurance Greater China Shipyards Tankers COSCO unveils massive supertanker fleet push Adis Ajdin November 10, 2026 0 671 3 minutes read Panjin Municipality Panjin Municipality Chinese tanker giant COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation has unveiled a sweeping fleet expansion involving 24 VLCC newbuildings, signing contracts worth RMB9.48bn ($1.42bn) for ten supertankers and lining up another 14 through long-term bareboat charters. The Shanghai- and Hong Kong-listed owner disclosed the deals on November 9, with its wholly owned subsidiary Hainan Cosco Shipping Energy Transportation placing orders at two Chinese shipyards. Six VLCCs have been contracted at Yangzhou COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry for RMB5.69bn ($853m), while Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Corporation (DSIC) has secured four vessels worth RMB3.79bn ($569m). The contracts are priced at approximately RMB948m ($142m) per ship, with the Yangzhou series scheduled for delivery between August 2029 and November 2030. The four DSIC vessels are due between September 2029 and May 2030. The Yangzhou newbuildings will feature LNG-ready fuel systems, while the DSIC quartet will be designed for future conversion to LNG or methanol dual-fuel propulsion. The Yangzhou deal is classified as a related-party transaction because the shipyard belongs to the COSCO group and still requires shareholder approval. The DSIC contract has received board approval without requiring a further shareholder vote. Alongside the direct newbuilding investment, COSCO Shipping Energy has approved plans to take another 14 VLCC newbuildings on bareboat charter from six Chinese financial leasing companies. The programme, handled through subsidiary Huanyu Shipowning, carries maximum rental commitments of RMB17.4bn ($2.61bn) over charter periods of up to 20 years. Bank of Communications Financial Leasing will provide four LNG dual-fuel VLCCs, while ICBC Financial Leasing will supply three. Agricultural Bank of China Financial Leasing is lined up for three conventionally powered vessels, with Bank of China Financial Leasing providing another one.CITIC Financial Leasing will contribute two LNG dual-fuel vessels, while Minsheng Financial Leasing will provide the remaining ship. The charter programme comprises ten LNG dual-fuel and four conventionally powered VLCCs, with all 14 vessels expected to enter service during 2030. The leasing arrangements still require shareholder approval, with the company opting for the bareboat structure to expand its operating fleet while limiting upfront capital expenditure. Taken together, the announcements cover ten directly ordered VLCCs and another 14 planned chartered newbuildings, marking a major expansion of Cosco Shipping Energy’s crude tanker fleet heading into the next decade. Separately, the company’s board has approved another proposal involving long-term leasing and financing arrangements for 16 VLCC newbuildings. The related-party proposal, which also requires shareholder approval, has yet to be accompanied by details of financing partners, shipyards, contract values or delivery schedules. The company said further information would be disclosed once specific agreements are signed, leaving it unclear whether the 16 vessels represent additional fleet expansion or overlap with other newbuilding plans. The proposed charters will run for up to 20 years, with the ships scheduled to enter the fleet during 2030.The largest allocation is four LNG dual-fuel VLCCs from Bank of Communications Financial Leasing, carrying a maximum combined rental commitment of RMB5.2bn ($779m). ICBC Financial Leasing will provide three LNG dual-fuel vessels, Agricultural Bank of China Financial Leasing three conventionally powered VLCCs, and Bank of China Financial Leasing one conventional vessel. CITIC Financial Leasing is lined up for two LNG dual-fuel ships, with Minsheng Financial Leasing providing another one. The arrangement covers ten LNG dual-fuel vessels and four conventionally powered VLCCs, although the broader specifications also refer to fuel-ready technologies. Cosco Shipping Energy said the bareboat structure would allow it to expand its fleet without the same level of upfront capital expenditure required for direct ship ownership. The programme was approved by the company’s board on November 9 but still requires shareholder approval because its cumulative leasing transactions over the previous 12 months exceed 50% of audited net assets. The announcement came alongside the company’s separate RMB9.48bn investment in ten owned VLCC newbuildings at Yangzhou Cosco Shipping Heavy Industry and Dalian Shipbuilding Industry, taking the group’s newly announced potential fleet additions to 24 supertankers. articles.title: Get your data in order and set a course for greener shipping
articles.summary: There is cause for optimism in the shipping sector, and we are seeing more and more initiatives aimed at making shipping greener. Shipowners are now far more willing to reduce emissions from ships than they were just a few years ago. That said, we must also acknowledge that the shipping industry has a data problem, […]
articles.body: There is cause for optimism in the shipping sector, and we are seeing more and more initiatives aimed at making shipping greener. Shipowners are now far more willing to reduce emissions from ships than they were just a few years ago. That said, we must also acknowledge that the shipping industry has a data problem, which means shipowners are not getting the insights needed to accelerate the green transition. In the coming weeks alone, there are two events worth keeping an eye on. From 23 to 27 November, the IMO’s working group known as ISWG-GHG 23 will continue its discussions on a global Net-Zero Framework – that is, proposals for common, global climate rules designed to steer the shipping industry towards net-zero emissions by 2050. A few days later, from 30 November to 3 December, the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) will convene for MEPC 85, with emissions, energy efficiency and environmental protection, amongst other topics, on the agenda. There remains disagreement over the way forward, but the work being done within the IMO, amongst others, demonstrates a willingness to find common solutions. I sense the same willingness when I speak to shipping companies and other industry stakeholders. Compared with just three years ago, there is far greater interest in concrete climate action. However, although progress is being made, the shipping industry still has a data problem. We still know too little about the emissions of individual ships and how they can reduce their fuel consumption. Far too many people still rely on calculations that are, at best, uncertain and, at worst, misleading. Shipowners cannot navigate between new requirements and regulations blindfolded. They need valid data to set the right course. Calculations and standard values do not reveal how engines perform during operation or how high emissions really are. In the coming years, shipping companies will have to deal with the use of multiple fuels, technologies and types of emissions. How do they assess emissions from different fuels whilst at sea? How do they demonstrate that an investment reduces emissions? And how do they determine the engine settings that deliver the lowest fuel consumption? Here, real-time measurements are a crucial tool – for documentation, compliance with requirements and day-to-day decision-making. The new five-year partnership between the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) and Equinor is a strong example of how the green transition requires joint efforts and practical trials. They will collaborate on areas including alternative fuels, energy efficiency and CO₂ management. Their emphasis on documentation and verification is entirely appropriate. After all, shipowners and organisations can only derive the full benefit from such initiatives if they have access to valid data. I therefore hope that they will involve experts in emissions measurement to a greater extent at an early stage of the process. This increases the likelihood that we can actually learn from each other’s experiences. At the same time, shipowners can take advantage of some straightforward opportunities. Linking real-time measurements to the engines’ operational data would enable shipping companies to identify which operating conditions increase fuel consumption and emissions. However, without the necessary equipment on board, these opportunities are easily overlooked. With valid data, shipping companies can act immediately to reduce costs and cut emissions. I hope that the IMO meetings will bring the shipping industry closer to achieving common climate regulations. However, these regulations cannot stand alone. The green course must be set collectively and guided by what we can measure and document. Rene B. Christensen, CEO, Green Instruments, Denmark
takeaways: There is cause for optimism in the shipping sector, and we are seeing more and more initiatives aimed at making shipping greener.
Shipowners are now far more willing to reduce emissions from ships than they were just a few years ago.
That said, we must also acknowledge that the shipping industry has a data problem, which means shipowners are not getting the insights needed to accelerate the green transition.

articles.body: Finance and Insurance Operations Poseidon Principles broadens industry engagement with new council Sam Chambers November 10, 2026 0 89 1 minute read PPMI PPMI The Poseidon Principles has assembled an advisory council drawn from across the shipping industry, appointing Watson Farley & Williams managing partner Lindsey Keeble as its chair. The 16-member council includes Navios boss Angeliki Frangou, Seaspan chairman Bing Chen, Pacific Basin CEO Martin Fruergaard, Höegh Autoliners chief Andreas Enger and GasLog CFO Achilleas Tasioulas. Other prominent names include Star Bulk’s Charis Plakontonaki, DNV’s Knut Ørbeck-Nilssen, Knutsen’s Synnøve Seglem, Cargill’s James Lewis and MOL Europe’s Bruce Moore. Established earlier this year, the council will meet two to three times annually, providing shipowners and other maritime stakeholders with a direct channel to influence the development of the Poseidon Principles, the shipping finance industry’s principal climate alignment framework. Launched in 2019, the initiative now has 36 financial institution signatories representing nearly three-quarters of global ship finance. It requires lenders to assess and disclose how their shipping portfolios align with the IMO’s greenhouse gas reduction ambitions. Keeble said the council would help ensure the principles remain “practical, relevant and effective” as shipping navigates its energy transition. The appointment comes as the association considers broadening its remit beyond emissions, with crew welfare emerging as a priority for future work. Council members will serve two-year terms, with the current appointments running until 2028. articles.summary: South Korea has given conditional approval for the sale of Hyundai LNG Shipping to Indonesia’s Sinar Mas Group, removing the final regulatory hurdle in a deal that has been held up for months by national energy security concerns. articles.body: Asia Gas South Korea clears Sinar Mas takeover of Hyundai LNG Shipping Sam Chambers November 10, 2026 0 210 1 minute read Hyundai LNG Shipping Hyundai LNG Shipping South Korea has given conditional approval for the sale of Hyundai LNG Shipping to Indonesia’s Sinar Mas Group, removing the final regulatory hurdle in a deal that has been held up for months by national energy security concerns. The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy has completed a foreign investment security review, approving the transaction subject to undisclosed national security conditions. The sellers, a consortium comprising IMM Private Equity and IMM Investment, are now targeting November 23 to complete the transaction, nearly a year after signing a sale agreement with Sinar Mas. The Indonesian conglomerate is acquiring the company through its Frontier Resources subsidiary for approximately KRW400bn ($275m), with the enterprise value, including debt, estimated at KRW3.8trn ($2.6bn). Hyundai LNG Shipping operates 12 LNG carriers and six LPG carriers and holds long-term transportation contracts with state-owned Korea Gas Corporation (KOGAS). The proposed foreign takeover has faced fierce opposition from South Korean shipowners, who warned that transferring control of strategically important gas carriers overseas could undermine national energy security and lead to the loss of maritime expertise. Sinar Mas has sought to address these concerns by pledging to maintain Korean-flag operations and protect existing employment. Hyundai LNG Shipping was carved out of Hyundai Merchant Marine, now HMM, in 2014. An attempt to sell the business back to HMM in 2023 collapsed over differences in valuation. The latest approval clears the way for IMM to exit its investment after 12 years. articles.body: Middle East Operations Best Oasis becomes second cash buyer to secure US sanctions clearance Sam Chambers November 10, 2026 0 169 1 minute read MarineTraffic / Hakon Rimmereid MarineTraffic / Hakon Rimmereid Dubai-based ship recycling cash buyer Best Oasis has secured authorisation from the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to negotiate deals involving sanctioned vessels, becoming the second company after GMS to receive such approval. The development opens another potential route for removing ageing ships from the sanctioned fleet, which has expanded rapidly as western governments have targeted vessels involved in transporting Iranian, Russian and Venezuelan oil. Best Oasis, headed by Gaurav Mehta, is one of the world’s largest cash buyers of end-of-life ships. The company was established in 2010 as an expansion of India’s Priya Blue ship recycling business. The authorisation allows Best Oasis to pursue negotiations, although individual transactions involving blocked vessels would still require the necessary OFAC clearance before they could be completed. The move follows a series of landmark approvals granted to rival GMS earlier this year. In May, Washington authorised GMS to acquire four sanctioned containerships linked to Iranian shipping magnate Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani for recycling. The vessels, Yogi, Timon, Rantanplan and Bigli, had been stranded following their designation under US sanctions last year. GMS subsequently secured approval in August to recycle two seized tankers, Marinera and Galileo, which had been taken into US custody during Washington’s crackdown on Venezuelan oil shipments. The growing willingness to license recycling transactions comes as sanctioned vessels account for an increasingly substantial share of the demolition market. articles.title: Container freight rates weaken as WCI and FBX extend declines
articles.summary: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly assessments, with Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) and the Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) recording further declines, while Chinese freight benchmarks and individual trade lanes showed contrasting movements. Drewry’s WCI decreased 1% to...
articles.body: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly assessments, with Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) and the Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) recording further declines, while Chinese freight benchmarks and individual trade lanes showed contrasting movements. Drewry’s WCI decreased 1% to US$4,389 per 40-foot container, while the FBX Global Container Freight Index fell 2% to US$3,452. Both benchmarks declined for a second consecutive week, following the increases recorded earlier in October. Meanwhile, the China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) rose 2.28%, contrasting with declines in the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI). The NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) also presented a mixed picture, with Asia-US West Coast recording an increase while the other four monitored trade lanes declined. Chinese freight indexes move in different directions The SCFI declined 1.46% to 3,633.45 points on 6 November, compared with 3,687.35 in the previous assessment. The CCFI moved in the opposite direction, increasing approximately 2.28% to 1,924.69 points from 1,881.82 a week earlier. The increase reversed the relatively modest movement recorded in the preceding assessment. The NCFI declined approximately 1.93% to 2,443.24 points, compared with 2,491.26 previously, marking a second consecutive weekly decrease. The divergence between the three Chinese benchmarks indicates that their latest assessments did not reflect a uniform market direction. NYFI shows mixed Transpacific movements The NYFI assessment published on 6 November recorded an increase on Asia-US West Coast, while Asia-US East Coast declined marginally. Asia-US West Coast rose 1.29% to 7,823.86 from 7,724.52, extending the upward movement recorded in the previous assessment. Asia-US East Coast decreased 0.23% to 10,101.42, compared with 10,125.18 a week earlier. The contrasting movements suggest that the two major Transpacific routes continued to experience different short-term developments, although the East Coast decline remained relatively limited. Asia-North Europe fell 1.04% to 3,170.40 from 3,203.78, reversing the 5.40% increase recorded in the preceding assessment. The latest movement indicates renewed weakness on the route following its brief recovery. Transatlantic rates decline in both directions The Transatlantic market recorded decreases in both directions in the latest NYFI assessment. Westbound rates declined 3.57% to 2,840.25 from 2,945.35, reversing the previous week’s 2.19% increase. Eastbound rates fell more sharply, decreasing 5.86% to 1,058.39 from 1,124.31. The Eastbound decline followed an 18.77% increase in the preceding assessment, illustrating the considerable week-to-week volatility affecting the route. Both Transatlantic directions therefore returned to negative territory, contributing to the broader weakness observed across four of the five NYFI trade lanes. Drewry WCI falls for a second consecutive week Drewry’s WCI declined 1% to US$4,389 per 40-foot container in its assessment published on 5 November, compared with US$4,429 in the previous week. On the Transpacific, Shanghai-Los Angeles remained broadly unchanged at US$7,539 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-New York declined 3% to US$9,303. On Asia-Europe, Shanghai-Rotterdam decreased 2% to US$3,615 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-Genoa remained broadly stable at US$4,166. The latest assessment followed a 3% decline in the WCI during the preceding week, when weaker Transpacific rates contributed to the overall decrease. Drewry also highlighted capacity developments affecting the container shipping market, including the potential implications of more vessels returning to Suez Canal routes. A wider return to shorter transit routes could affect effective vessel capacity and network deployment, although the scale and timing of any market impact will depend on carrier decisions and operating conditions. These developments remain relevant to the freight rate outlook but should not be interpreted as the confirmed cause of the latest weekly movements. FBX Global Index continues downward The FBX Global Container Freight Index declined 2% to US$3,452, compared with US$3,513 in the preceding assessment. The decrease followed a 1% decline a week earlier, extending the downward movement in the global benchmark. The latest FBX reading therefore aligned with the negative direction of Drewry’s WCI, although the two indexes use different methodologies and underlying market data. Their simultaneous declines suggest softer conditions across the global freight markets captured by these benchmarks, even as the CCFI recorded an increase. Diverging benchmarks underline an uneven market The latest assessments highlight substantial differences between global composite benchmarks and individual trade-lane developments. Drewry’s WCI and the FBX declined for a second consecutive week, while the SCFI and NCFI also moved lower. However, the CCFI increased 2.28%, demonstrating that weakness was not reflected across every Chinese benchmark. On the Transpacific, NYFI Asia-US West Coast increased 1.29%, while Drewry’s Shanghai-Los Angeles assessment remained broadly unchanged. For US East Coast routes, both indexes indicated softer conditions, with NYFI Asia-US East Coast declining 0.23% and Drewry Shanghai-New York falling 3%. On Asia-Europe, the latest readings were more closely aligned. NYFI Asia-North Europe declined 1.04%, while Drewry Shanghai-Rotterdam decreased 2%. Nevertheless, comparisons between the two indexes require caution because their methodologies, route definitions and reporting periods differ. Market outlook The latest figures indicate continued downward pressure on several major container freight benchmarks, although the direction and scale of movements remain uneven. The second consecutive weekly declines in Drewry’s WCI and the FBX suggest that the recovery recorded earlier in October has lost momentum. At the same time, the increase in the CCFI and continued gains on NYFI Asia-US West Coast demonstrate that the market is not experiencing a uniform decline. articles.title: The dirty secret of shipping’s clean hull ambitions
articles.summary: Hull fouling drives up fuel bills and emissions, yet ports increasingly restrict the very cleaning operations needed to tackle it. The missing piece is a global network of places where ships can safely get cleaned. Alex Byelyavtsev explains. A dirty hull burns more fuel. Cleaning reduces resistance and emissions....
articles.body: Contributions Operations The dirty secret of shipping’s clean hull ambitions Splash November 10, 2026 0 150 3 minutes read EcoSubsea EcoSubsea Hull fouling drives up fuel bills and emissions, yet ports increasingly restrict the very cleaning operations needed to tackle it. The missing piece is a global network of places where ships can safely get cleaned. Alex Byelyavtsev explains. A dirty hull burns more fuel. Cleaning reduces resistance and emissions. Cleaning can also release organisms, coating particles, biocides and microplastics into the water. So ports restrict it. Once cleaning is restricted, the ship may keep sailing with the dirty hull. More resistance. More fuel. More emissions. Each instruction can be reasonable. Together they create an operating problem. Where is the ship supposed to clean the hull when performance starts deteriorating, while remaining inside biosecurity rules, pollution controls, coating limits, terminal restrictions and the commercial schedule? The missing technology may not be the cleaning machine. It may be the network of places where that machine can actually be used. IMO-linked research has put a number on the fuel case. In the scenario studied, a slime layer as thin as 0.5 millimetres covering up to half a hull can raise greenhouse-gas emissions by about 25 to 30%, depending on ship type, speed and conditions. Extra shaft power is extra fuel. That fuel was already a bunker cost. Under CII and, where it applies, EU ETS, it can also move the rating and the allowance bill. Cleaning does not automatically make fouling disappear. Without capture, it transfers it into the surrounding water. Aggressive cleaning can also damage the antifouling system. So a second instruction appears: do not contaminate the port. The same ship has to follow both. That is already visible in operations. Gard recorded a vessel on a short time charter, first voyage from Malaysia toward New Plymouth. New Zealand authorities rejected it for biofouling non-compliance. Owners diverted to Bundaberg, Australia, for hull cleaning. Bad weather meant the ship reached New Zealand about three weeks late and missed the laycan. Charterers had to find other business. The ship had to find an acceptable cleaning option before it could complete the intended voyage. A second Gard case in the same note is sharper. A vessel had already undergone underwater inspection and cleaning in West Africa before a New Zealand call. MPI still found the evidence on the sea chest insufficient and issued a Notice of Direction. Extra work had to be arranged before arrival. Cleaning is not always the same as a regulator accepting that the ship is clean. The market already wrote that geography into the contract. Under BIMCO’s 2019 Hull Fouling Clause for time charters, where the clause applies and cleaning is called for following an inspection, speed and consumption warranties can remain suspended if cleaning at the place of inspection is not permitted or possible. Paint manufacturers’ guidelines still apply. The clause assumes the fouling. It does not assume a berth. Delay has a fuel number. DNV, in April 2025, put light slime at up to 20% extra fuel consumption and heavy shell fouling at up to 85%. Those figures are not a promise for every ship. They are the cost of keeping a fouled hull in service while the vessel waits for a place where cleaning is permitted. The IMO revised its biofouling guidelines in 2023. In April 2025 it approved guidance on in-water cleaning. IMO itself says in-water cleaning can damage coatings, shorten coating life and release harmful substances and invasive species. If the answer were simply “clean the hull,” that circular would not be needed. In March 2026 ISO 6319 set requirements for how to plan, conduct and document in-water cleaning, including sea chests and other hull openings. It tells ports and operators how a clean can be done. It does not require a port to allow one. GreenVoyage2050 states the port barrier directly. Many ports do not allow hull and propeller cleaning during the stay. Barriers include discharge of biomass, lack of reception facilities, conflict with cargo and bunkering, diver safety, and permits that cleaning companies often cannot obtain. If cleaning costs time, the ship may later speed up to recover the schedule. Part of the efficiency gain can be eaten by the recovery. Singapore shows capability, not a finished network. In 2026 the Maritime and Port Authority selected six partners to trial robotic in-water inspection and cleaning under actual port conditions, from the second half of the year. MPA’s point is that commercial systems already exist. The hard part is running them alongside busy operations, currents, hull geometry and debris-capture rules. Commercial cleaning technologies exist. What is not yet established at global scale is the operating network around them. Better coatings matter. They do not answer the berth question. Idle time, warm water, route changes, sea chests and thrusters still produce fouling. From the ship the sequence is ordinary. This port does not allow in-water cleaning. The next port has no approved contractor, or capture of debris is required and the equipment is not there. The call is short. The ship departs with a dirty hull. Cleaning reduces resistance and emissions.

The Haugesund-based company disclosed that one of its wholly owned subsidiaries had received a statement of claim from Statnett concerning a tender process that did not result in a contract. articles.title: Dry Bulk Shipping: Thermal Coal Market Heating Up
articles.summary: Demand for thermal coal is growing once more, with shipping standing to benefit. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “with the winter heating season underway, the thermal coal market is benefiting from strengthening demand, as elevated natural gas prices reinforce coal’s cost competitiveness...
articles.body: Dry Bulk Shipping: Thermal Coal Market Heating Up in Hellenic Shipping News 10/11/2026 D emand for thermal coal is growing once more, with shipping standing to benefit. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “with the winter heating season underway, the thermal coal market is benefiting from strengthening demand, as elevated natural gas prices reinforce coal’s cost competitiveness in power generation. Qatari LNG volumes remain sharply reduced, while European natural gas prices have returned to levels last seen during the 2022 energy crisis, with Dutch TTF prices recently exceeding €100/MWh and EU gas inventories below their 5-year average. These conditions have improved coal-fired generation economics, encouraging gas-to-coal switching across parts of Europe and Asia. Nevertheless, seaborne thermal coal trade is expected to remain broadly stable in 2026, as additional demand from fuel switching is largely offset by supply constraints”. Source: Intermodal Shipbroker According to Intermodal’s Head of Research Department, Mr. Nikos Tagoulis, “beyond this short-term supportive backdrop, the broader outlook remains uncertain. China’s seaborne thermal coal imports are forecast to decline, pressured by elevated international prices and expectations of recovering domestic production. Although mine inspections and safety restrictions have constrained output in recent months, government directives to accelerate mining activity in Shanxi, which accounts for approximately 30% of Chinese coal production, point to improving domestic availability. Together with expanding renewable generation, this could further reduce China’s import requirements in 2027, while Japan and South Korea may also face longer-term demand slowdowns amid continued decarbonization efforts. Meanwhile, India and ASEAN economies, particularly Vietnam and the Philippines, remain drivers of coal consumption growth, supported by rising electricity demand and industrial activity. In India, weaker hydropower generation amid El Niño-linked monsoon shortfalls, increased industrial demand and restocking have supported seaborne imports, although government efforts to expand domestic coal production aim to reduce reliance on imported supplies”. “On the supply side, Indonesia, the world’s largest thermal coal exporter, continues to face constraints. Although production quotas were revised upwards in October, approved output remains well below last year’s levels. At the same time, domestic market obligations require miners to prioritise local supply, leaving fewer tons for export. Supply has been further squeezed by El Niño-driven low river levels in Central Kalimantan, which have limited barge movements to terminals, tightening export availability. Australia, which together with Indonesia accounts for close to 70% of global thermal coal exports, is expected to record broadly flat volumes, with limited upside as its traditional North Asian buyers are set to reduce imports over the medium term. As these conditions create opportunities for alternative suppliers, Colombia is strengthening its position in the Atlantic thermal coal market, benefiting from renewed European demand amid elevated natural gas prices. According to LSEG, European thermal coal imports surged 79% y-o-y in October, while cumulative imports rose 31% during January–October. Over the same ten-month period, Colombian shipments to Europe increased 46%, maintaining a market share of around 60% and underscoring the country’s importance as a key coal supplier”, Mr. Tagoulis noted. “Overall, Colombian thermal coal exports increased by approximately 11% during January-October and are poised for further growth of around 8% in 2027, although their geographical distribution has shifted. Weaker Asian demand has been offset by stronger purchases from European and regional Atlantic buyers. Mexico has emerged as a key destination, alongside growing demand from Central American and Caribbean markets, while firmer Indonesian prices have improved Colombian coal’s competitiveness. For dry bulk shipping, however, the benefits of expanding Colombian exports are somewhat tempered by evolving trade patterns. While higher shipment volumes support cargo demand, the increasing orientation towards Atlantic Basin destinations reduces average sailing distances compared with Asian routes, potentially constraining ton-mile growth relative to physical trade expansion”, Intermodal’s analyst said. Source: Intermodal Shipbroker “Furthermore, following last August’s change in administration, Colombia has adopted a more supportive stance towards the coal sector, reopening export channel to Israel by lifting the previous government’s ban and signalling renewed support for exploration and mining investment. Nevertheless, significant operational risks persist. Repeated attacks on the railway linking the Cerrejón mine to its coastal export terminal, including a derailment in late September, alongside recurring community blockades, continue to threaten the reliability of coal shipments. Despite these logistical and security challenges, Colombia is poised to expand its footprint in global coal exports, benefiting from favourable gas-to-coal economics, a near-term shift in energy demand towards coal and uncertainty surrounding Indonesian shipments, while a more conducive domestic policy environment helps it capitalize on emerging export opportunities”, Intermodal’s analyst concluded. articles.title: Somali Piracy Resurgence: Understanding The Risk To Commercial Shipping
articles.summary: In the Gulf of Aden, Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and Somali Basin, piracy has reemerged as a significant threat to commercial shipping. After a lull in piracy from 2012 to 2024, when incidents were limited to zero or a couple per year, piracy has begun to increase since 2024. This rise has accelerated further so far ...
articles.body: Somali Piracy Resurgence: Understanding The Risk To Commercial Shipping in International Shipping News 10/11/2026 In the Gulf of Aden, Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and Somali Basin, piracy has reemerged as a significant threat to commercial shipping. After a lull in piracy from 2012 to 2024, when incidents were limited to zero or a couple per year, piracy has begun to increase since 2024. This rise has accelerated further so far in 2026. The rise in piracy is driven by state weakness and diverted international naval efforts, which have increased pirates’ ability to operate. Moreover, weapons and finance networks that connect Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) logistics with Al-Shabaab, Houthis, and Pirate Action Groups (‘PAGs’) also incentivise piracy. Pirate activity represents a significant threat to commercial operations, both in Somali territorial waters and offshore. The financial objective of Somali pirates is to hijack vessels and then pressure the relevant stakeholders into providing the group with a ransom payment in exchange for the return of the crew/vessel. As the Houthis also play a major role in this network, they also assist pirate activity, especially in the Gulf of Aden. With the monsoon season recently ending, pirates have favourable weather conditions to use motherships to attack commercial vessels at a significant distance from the coast (up to several hundred nautical miles). In the late 2000s, piracy emerged as a significant issue in the Gulf of Aden and the Somali basin. At its peak, in 2011, over 230 attacks were recorded, with piracy costing shippers and governments around $7 billion during this period. The resurgence of piracy since 2024 threatens to similarly increase the costs to shippers and governments. In the period between January to September 2026, the International Maritime Bureau recorded a rise in Somali piracy activity, with 15 recorded incidents of Somali piracy. They also note that Somali pirates accounted for 94% of all crew taken hostage globally. The figures from international anti-piracy missions indicate that the rate of piracy incidents is likely even higher. On 24 August 2026, the Royal Navy reported that the international anti-piracy mission, Combined Task Force 151, had responded to 25 piracy-related incidents between 24 February and 24 August 2026. As of early November, the following successful hijackings/armed robberies have been recorded in the region: 15 Recorded Somali piracy incidents Jan-Sep 2026 | IMB 94% Share of crew taken hostage globally Attributed to Somali pirates | IMB 25 Piracy-related incidents handled 24 Feb-24 Aug 2026 | CTF 151 Consistent with historical trends, most piracy occurs in littoral areas because commercial vessels are easier to reach in these areas. Nevertheless, there has been a general increase in PAGs targeting highvalue tankers in the Gulf of Aden, likely in coordination with the Houthis, due to the high ransom payments that they can demand for these vessels. For example, Somali pirates are currently demanding $10 million in ransom for the release of the EUREKA and its crew. Stakeholders regularly struggle to pay these high ransom amounts. Consequently, an estimated 20 crew members, belonging to at least one vessel, remain hostage. This includes crew members that have been held several months after the hijacking date, including the crew of ASANA. During the recent surge in piracy, pirates have increased their use of large vessels as motherships (e.g. the cement carrier SWARD was repurposed as a mothership). Even though Somali pirates engage in cooperation with Al-Shabaab and the Houthis, the selection of targets does not demonstrate a clear pattern, as hijacked vessels have had a wide range of ownership. The recent hijacking of SIBU 1 shows this. Since the hijacking, its missing flag data has led to it continuing to be classified as having indeterminate ownership, although the vessel is believed to be part of the Iranian shadow fleet. Why has pirate activity returned? Over the last few years, the Somali Federal Government’s longstanding weaknesses in exerting control have further deteriorated, creating ideal conditions for piracy. In early 2026, officials in the South-West state announced their intention to sever ties with the Federal Government. This decision was primarily motivated by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s constitutional reforms to extend the presidential term, along with other changes. From the perspective of officials in the South-West state, and many others in the country, Mohamud’s reforms are an effort to restrict democracy. After the South-West state announced its desire to sever ties, the Federal Government seized control of Baidoa, the state’s administrative capital, in March 2026. Even after the government seized the city, intermittent clashes have continued in the city’s outskirts between the federal government and forces aligned with the state government. The potential loss of the South-West state poses a significant risk to the Federal Government’s authority, especially as it mirrors similar independence movements in recent years. For example, in 2024, the semi-autonomous state of Puntland announced it would begin operating independently of the federal government. In addition to these state-level secessionist movements, the federal government faces an ongoing threat from Al-Shabaab. Despite continued military operations against the group, Al-Shabaab remains in control of around 30% of Somalia, mainly in the south. With these multifaceted security threats, the government has been unable to adequately allocate resources to anti-piracy missions. Furthermore, the increased commercial traffic in the Somali basin has created increased opportunities for piracy to occur due to the increased volume of potential targets. The twofold maritime disruptions of Houthi attacks on the Red Sea and IRGC attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have caused a growing number of ships to reroute via the Cape of Good Hope and via the northeastern coast of Somalia. This rerouting has placed a higher percentage of vessels within the range of Somali pirate attacks. Conversely, vessel transits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden have declined by 60-70% in recent months, primarily as many shipping companies have bypassed this route due to the threat levels. In response to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, anti-piracy naval missions have reduced their scope. Various high-end units have been diverted from combating piracy to these other theatres. The primary international anti-piracy task force is the Combined Task Force 151, which operates broadly throughout the region. Moreover, the European Union’s anti-piracy mission, Operation ATALANTA, is also present in the region, and participates in coordinated exercises/patrols with the Combined Force 151. This mission’s mandate extends until February 2027. The EU is yet to confirm whether it will be extended beyond this date. However, it will likely be renewed due to the high rates of piracy. While these missions play a valuable role in addressing piracy, they have failed to prevent the current increase in piracy In the anti-piracy missions in 2011, and the following several years, piracy was nearly eliminated by the operation of up to 30 warships simultaneously operating through three overlapping missions. Contrastingly, the EU’s Operation Atalanta is limited to roughly two vessels and air assets deployed simultaneously, while some Combined Task Force 151 assets have been diverted to the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea. Although the extent of the diversions is currently unknown. The reduced scale of these missions has prevented them from effectively covering the wide geographic area where piracy occurs. In recent months, the resource limitations have worsened as ship diversions have caused vessels to undertake fewer dedicated escort or patrol days in the traditional IRTC/Somali Basin area. In response to these issues, countries adhering to the Djibouti Code of Conduct Task Force signed a proposal in July 2026 to establish a task force to enhance existing anti-piracy efforts. The exact scope and details of this task force are still being determined. Somalia signed a pivotal 10-year bilateral Defence and Economic Cooperation Agreement with Türkiye in 2024, which includes Turkish assistance in anti-piracy measures. Although this agreement can help with piracy to an extent, it cannot comprehensively combat piracy. Turkish anti-piracy assistance does not replace ongoing missions, as it mainly relates to hostage recovery. Unlike international anti-piracy missions that seek to deter and proactively stop pirate activity through an ongoing presence. Implications for owners, charterers, underwriters Currently, the risk to shipowners, charters, and underwriters is significant in the Gulf of Aden and the Somali Basin, with multiple crews held and regular pirate activity in these waters. In the near-term, this risk is expected to heighten further. The recent Houthi activity in Yemen indicates the increasing dual threat environment in the Gulf of Aden. In September 2026, Houthi forces launched a major operation throughout southwestern Yemen wherein they captured around 5,400 square kilometres of territory along the strategically significant southwest coast. The Houthis’ seizures include the valuable port city of Mocha, which is located around 80km north of the Bab el-Mandeb, and Perim Island within the Bab el-Mandeb strait. With the Houthis improved strategic position on the Bab el-Mandeb, they will likely seek to coordinate with Somali pirate groups to solidify the dual threat environment. The Houthis can utilise cooperation with PAGs to disrupt shipping along the Gulf of Aden and disrupt the southern entrance to the Bab el-Mandeb, especially vis-à-vis Saudi Arabian shipping. In doing so, the Houthis can enhance their capacity to extract concessions from Saudi Arabia. However, the Houthis control over the Bab el-Mandeb has been constrained to an extent by the Saudibacked Presidential Leadership Council’s (‘PLC’) Operation Dawn of Yemen. Launched in September 2026, the operation has recaptured key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb, including the port city of Mocha on 5 October 2026. Houthi forces have denied PLC claims that they recaptured the city. Additionally, on 6 October 2026, Türkiye and Pakistan announced they are sending troops to assist Saudi Arabia in the conflict, in accordance with their mutual defence agreement. As these forces will concentrate their efforts on Yemen and the northern side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to repel the Houthis, it may facilitate a further increase in piracy; this is especially the case if Turkish resources are diverted from Somalia to Yemen. Over the next few months, anti-piracy mission will affect the risk to commercial shipping. While the European Union will likely renew Operation ATALANTA beyond February 2027, the mission’s scale will influence the piracy threat. If the EU increases the number of assets deployed as part of this mission, it will assist in addressing the continued issues with the diversion of Combined Task Force 151 resources. Even though Operation ATALANTA and Combined Task Force 151 continue to play an important role in antipiracy operations, they cannot address piracy alone. Throughout 2026, the Somalian Government has repeatedly called on greater coordinated international action to address the rise in piracy. Thus far, these appeals have been largely ignored; instead, the international community continues to overlook piracy in favour of other pressing geopolitical concerns. Ostensibly, the newly formed Djibouti Code of Conduct Task Force (consisting of 22 signatory member states across the Western Indian Ocean and surrounding regions), is an answer to these requests. However, it is unlikely that the mission will be sufficient to address the shortfall in anti-piracy resources. The signatory states, in general, lack the economic or naval resources to divert to addressing piracy at the required scale. Ultimately, owners, charterers, and underwriters face a high-risk environment. This is largely driven by inadequate anti-piracy measures throughout the region and expanded Houthi-pirate coordination, which has created a dual-threat environment in the Gulf of Aden. takeaways: After a lull in piracy from 2012 to 2024, when incidents were limited to zero or a couple per year, piracy has begun to increase since 2024.
This rise has accelerated further so far in 2026.
The rise in piracy is driven by state weakness and diverted international naval efforts, which have increased pirates’ ability to operate.

articles.title: Listening is not enough to protect seafarers’ mental health
articles.summary: The maritime industry has become much better at asking seafarers how they feel. The harder question is whether it is prepared to act on what they say. Surveys, welfare reports and personal testimony have brought mental health out of the margins of maritime debate, but listening has value only when seafarers’ lived...
articles.body: Listening is not enough to protect seafarers’ mental health in International Shipping News 10/11/2026 T he maritime industry has become much better at asking seafarers how they feel. The harder question is whether it is prepared to act on what they say. Surveys, welfare reports and personal testimony have brought mental health out of the margins of maritime debate, but listening has value only when seafarers’ lived experiences lead to practical changes onboard. The Mission to Seafarers’ Seafarers Happiness Index draws directly on accounts of life and work at sea. The International Transport Workers’ Federation, the International Seafarers’ Welfare and Assistance Network and other organisations also use frontline experience to identify risks and recommend improvements. This work has made it harder to dismiss loneliness, fatigue, anxiety or burnout as private matters that seafarers must manage alone. The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006, as amended, affirms every seafarer’s right to a safe and secure workplace, decent working and living conditions, health protection and welfare measures. It provides a clear basis for treating mental health as part of occupational safety and decent work, not an optional addition to crew welfare. The challenge is to make those protections visible in everyday life onboard. Yet a persistent distance remains between policy and daily life. Rules, corporate commitments and data will not protect a seafarer whose rest is routinely disrupted, whose contract is repeatedly extended or whose access to family depends on unreliable or costly connectivity. In a study conducted by the Maritime Authority of Jamaica, one participant said that shipowners appeared to value the cargo more than the person responsible for delivering it. The remark exposes a contradiction at the centre of global trade. Seafarers are indispensable, yet the human cost of sustaining the system is too often treated as secondary to schedules, productivity and commercial pressure. Meaningful change must begin with working conditions. Fatigue cannot be solved by a wellbeing poster or helpline if the work patterns that create it remain untouched. Rest hours must be enforced, not merely recorded for compliance, and rotation schedules must reduce prolonged fatigue and burnout. Commercial demands cannot routinely override safeguards intended to protect seafarers. Dawn Doyley, Registrar of Seafarers, Maritime Authority of Jamaica Connectivity and shore leave are equally important. Free, dependable communication helps seafarers maintain relationships and seek support before distress reaches a crisis point. Shore leave offers relief from the confined environment of the vessel and the unbroken routine of onboard duties. Both are basic contributors to wellbeing, not privileges granted only when operations permit. Mental health support must become a normal feature of life at sea. Regular check-ups, confidential access to qualified services onboard and ashore, and practical programmes on stress and coping should be built into employment. Support must be accessible, culturally aware and protected against stigma or professional disadvantage. Leadership onboard will determine whether those services are utilised effectively. Masters, senior officers and managers need training to recognise distress and respond with empathy, discretion and respect. Seafarers will not speak openly where vulnerability is treated as weakness or seeking help appears to threaten future employment. Trust must therefore be reinforced by clear confidentiality safeguards. An inclusive culture is part of effective risk management. Seafarers have always shown extraordinary resilience under demanding conditions, but resilience must not become an excuse for leaving people to absorb pressures the system can reduce. Responsibility is shared by shipowners, managers, States, regulators, training institutions and welfare organisations. The industry already has substantial evidence from seafarers and need not wait for another crisis. Progress should be judged by what changes onboard: genuine rest, humane rotations, reliable communication, shore leave, confidential support and leaders who make it safe to ask for help. Seafarers’ voices are shaping the mental health conversation, but conversation is not the destination. The test is whether their experiences influence decisions, budgets, work patterns and leadership behaviour. That is how listening becomes accountability. If the maritime sector values the people who keep global trade moving, it must turn what it hears into conditions that allow them to work safely and with dignity. articles.body: Iran Expands Its Use of Fraudulent Ship Registries to Evade Sanctions in International Shipping News 10/11/2026 Nearly 300 Iranian-Linked Ships Sail Under Fraudulent Flags Nearly 300 Iranian-linked ships have been tracked using fraudulent ship registries over the past 90 days to evade sanctions, an accelerating issue that triggered an OFAC alert alongside sanctions imposed on key enablers and companies. Russia has largely discontinued using fraudulent ship registries for sanctions-evading tankers over 2026 as they are ‘stateless’ and thus vulnerable to naval boarding and interdiction. However, Iran has not only increased the number of ships using fraudulent ship registries but has expanded their use beyond tankers to other vessel types over the past 18 months. Windward Tracks 278 Ships Across 23 Fraudulent Registries Windward identified 278 ships that have broadcast flags of 23 fraudulent ship registries while sailing in the Middle East Gulf, Indian Ocean, and Gulf of Oman from August 6 to November 5. The top fraudulent ship registry used is Nicaragua (53 ships), followed by Anguilla (39) and Netherland Caribbean (27). • 68% of ships using fraudulent registries were tankers (190), of which 171 were sanctioned. • 22 of the 38 general cargo ships are flagged with the false Anguilla ship registry (58%), as are 10 of the 11 landing craft, including one naval landing craft. Mozambique has the other. Only 2 of Anguilla’s 39 vessels are tankers. • The average age of vessels identified using the fraudulent ship registries was 26 years • Guyana was used as the flag for five of the seven containerships identified. • LPG tankers comprised 17% of ships. There were 268 vessels identified using fraudulent ship registries in the same region in the year-ago period, but the number of cargo vessels has more than tripled (to 38 from 11). The number of tankers is down (222 vs. 190 now), but the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports, in place since mid-July, has seen many tankers leave the area. OFAC Targets a Network Selling Fraudulent Flags to Iranian Ships Vessel owners and operators evading U.S. sanctions and trading Iranian-origin petroleum or petrochemicals have increasingly relied on false flags to continue operating, OFAC said in its November 4 alert. The alert noted the use of false flags had increased since April 2025 when it warned of flag hopping within Iran’s shadow fleet. OFAC targeted 13 individuals and companies, most based in Chandigarh, India, that it said formed a criminal network selling fraudulent flags to Iranian ships. India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, formed companies that posed as the flag registries and maritime service providers of countries and jurisdictions including Guyana, Eswatini, Aruba, Mali, Mozambique, Malawi, Sint Maarten, and Timor-Leste, OFAC said. These companies sold fraudulent registrations and certificates to vessels carrying illicit Iranian oil. Source: Windward 2026-11-10 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Russia has largely discontinued using fraudulent ship registries for sanctions-evading tankers over 2026 as they are ‘stateless’ and thus vulnerable to naval boarding and interdiction.
However, Iran has not only increased the number of ships using fraudulent ship registries but has expanded their use beyond tankers to other vessel types over the past 18 months.
The top fraudulent ship registry used is Nicaragua (53 ships), followed by Anguilla (39) and Netherland Caribbean (27).

The Institute’s Ship Energy and Environment Special Interest...
articles.body: Ahead of MEPC85, IMarEST members highlight barriers to Net-Zero delivery in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 10/11/2026 Ahead of MEPC85, the Institute of Marine Engineering, Science and Technology (IMarEST) says its members now identify delivery, infrastructure, and value-chain coordination as the sector’s biggest barriers when it comes to IMO 2023 Greenhouse Gas strategy. The Institute’s Ship Energy and Environment Special Interest Group (SEESIG) gathered views from professionals across ship management, classification societies, engineering, science, academia and maritime services. They found little opposition to the IMO’s ambition of achieving Net-Zero emissions from international shipping. Instead, respondents overwhelmingly identified issues including infrastructure readiness, commercial incentives, fuel availability and the distribution of responsibility across the maritime value chain as the most significant barriers to the progress they are seeking. Alasdair Wishart, director of technical and policy at the IMarEST commented: “We are not seeing opposition to the Net-Zero Framework, or to decarbonisation as a principle. This is extremely encouraging as the industry seeks clarity at MEPC85. In fact, our industry snapshot suggests that marine professionals are now increasingly focussing on whether the transition can be delivered at the pace required.” Respondents expressed confidence in a range of potential decarbonisation pathways, including low and zero-carbon fuels, energy efficiency technologies, and operational improvements. However, many highlighted uncertainties around fuel production, bunkering infrastructure, supply chains and long-term regulatory frameworks as factors slowing investment decisions. Alasdair Wishart at the IMO They also pointed to growing recognition that maritime decarbonisation cannot be delivered without increased collaboration in the industry. Participants highlighted the need for greater coordination between shipowners, operators, ports, fuel producers, charterers, cargo owners and policymakers to unlock emissions reductions across the sector. Significantly, respondents identified operational measures such as voyage optimisation, digitalisation and just-in-time arrivals as among the most effective opportunities for reducing emissions in the near term. These findings suggest progress can be achieved today while longer-term fuel and propulsion solutions continue to scale. Alasdair continued: “Shipping has a unique opportunity to take control of its emissions and accelerate the transition to Net-Zero. The cost of inaction is greater than the cost of action, and many of the technologies needed to reduce emissions already exist or are advancing rapidly. “But we are seeing that the sector requires answers on how to create the conditions needed for investment confidence for fuels and infrastructure, as well as facilitation to kickstart collaboration on decarbonisation across the sector.” If this sample of IMarEST members is representative of wider industry sentiment, the commitment to achieving Net-Zero by 2050 is firmly established. The question that IMarEST members are now asking is how quickly practical barriers can be removed in order to deliver it. Source: IMarEST 2026-11-10 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd and Inmarsat Maritime: a case study in connected shipping
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd, the world’s fifth-largest container carrier, operates 300 vessels on 133 liner services, transporting 13.5 million twenty-foot-equivalent units a year between 600 ports worldwide. Given the scale and complexity of these operations, every decision affects thousands of containers per vessel – with the...
articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd, the world’s fifth-largest container carrier, operates 300 vessels on 133 liner services, transporting 13.5 million twenty-foot-equivalent units a year between 600 ports worldwide. Given the scale and complexity of these operations, every decision affects thousands of containers per vessel – with the consequences of any misstep felt throughout the supply chain. The company’s proactive approach to fleetwide digitalisation has therefore been devised with one overarching objective in mind: to simplify its operations. According to Patrick Briest, Hapag-Lloyd’s Senior Director of Operations and IT Products, digitalisation “can do many things”, but making things simpler – from both a commercial and operational perspective – is its one “superpower”. Digitalisation and the connectivity that supports it are increasingly judged by concrete commercial and operational outcomes. “We don’t digitalise just because we can,” Briest told the audience at a recent Inmarsat ‘Connected to Perform’ seminar during SMM 2026. “We digitalise because there’s a use case for it – because there’s value we can drive.” For Hapag-Lloyd, tangible targets include maintaining schedule reliability above 90% across its network, reducing emissions per TEU by 30% by 2030, and approaching net-zero emissions by 2045 – all while cutting operating costs by approximately $100 per TEU. Achieving these goals will require tapping into the “superpower” of digitalisation to facilitate faster and better-informed decisions, said Briest: “We want to enable ourselves, our people, to decide faster, decide better – because we’ve got the data and the tools to understand the impact of every one of the little operational decisions we make all the time.” To illustrate the benefits of digitalisation and connectivity on Hapag-Lloyd’s operations, Briest presented a notional voyage involving a container ship transporting perishable goods from the west coast of South America to Northern Europe. If a crane were to fail during the vessel’s final port call in South America, he said, the consequent delays might result in the ship missing its slot to cross the Panama Canal. However, by retrieving operational data from the vessel’s digital cargo logbook, Hapag-Lloyd would know by exactly how long to extend its port call to maximise cargo intake without sacrificing its slot. Later, if the vessel were to encounter extreme weather in the Atlantic Ocean, the operator would combine specific vessel data points with shore-based analysis to evaluate routing, speed, fuel consumption, and port arrival options. In this way, Briest explained, Hapag-Lloyd could keep commercial and environmental impacts to a minimum without compromising voyage safety. Digitalisation and connectivity, then, enable shipping companies like Hapag-Lloyd to make smarter operational decisions based on a richer and more immediate view of what is happening on the vessel and across the network. As Briest demonstrated in the second scenario, they also help close the gap between ship and shore. In another example, IT support teams can now connect directly with the vessel, remotely accessing even the engine room to help resolve technical issues efficiently. Whereas ships previously operated as isolated assets, they increasingly function as an extension of head office, with seafarers and shore staff working as one team, and the Atlantic Ocean – in Briest’s words – becoming “as connected as downtown Frankfurt”. Digitalisation is connecting vessels not only to their operator’s headquarters but also with the clients whose goods they transport. In a further operational scenario from the notional voyage, Briest explained that the Hapag-Lloyd LIVE tool allows customers to monitor refrigerated cargo and respond when circumstances change. If the vessel is delayed, temperature settings can be adjusted remotely to help ensure the cargo reaches its destination in optimal condition. “By being more digital, we want to be as easy to do business with for our customers as we possibly can be,” he commented. Recognising that increased connectivity also has its challenges, Hapag-Lloyd’s digitalisation strategy emphasises cybersecurity and seafarer autonomy to maintain operational resilience. “As we connect more systems on the vessel, we’re of course creating a substantially bigger attack surface,” Briest acknowledged, adding that the company is “pushing between 100 and 200 patches to every vessel every week” to address this issue. Cybersecurity, he said, “cannot be an afterthought anymore” – instead, it should be “secure by design and [built] from the ground up”. At the same time, Hapag-Lloyd is taking care to ensure digitalisation strengthens rather than weakens the judgement, resilience, and practical competency of its seafarers. “Digitalisation can help a lot, but there’s an inherent [seafaring] culture, capability and skillset that we also need to preserve,” said Briest. These considerations become increasingly important as Hapag-Lloyd’s digitalisation strategy progresses. As more decisions, systems, applications, and interactions come to depend on the ship–shore connection, and the vessel is further integrated into the broader digital operating environment, connectivity itself becomes strategic infrastructure. Inmarsat Maritime’s NexusWave is a key enabler of Hapag-Lloyd’s digitalisation strategy. The fully managed, bonded multi-network connectivity solution delivers the consistent high speeds, global reliability, and secure-by-design infrastructure the company needs to continue its transformation and pursue its operational ambitions with confidence. Digitalisation, Briest summarised, is helping Hapag-Lloyd to manage its workload, make better decisions, and work more effectively as a team – both onboard the vessel and between ship and shore. While he stressed that connectivity needs to be managed responsibly to preserve cybersecurity and crew autonomy, he was in no doubt about the direction of travel: “The future of shipping is connected,” he concluded.
takeaways: Hapag-Lloyd, the world’s fifth-largest container carrier, operates 300 vessels on 133 liner services, transporting 13.5 million twenty-foot-equivalent units a year between 600 ports worldwide.
Given the scale and complexity of these operations, every decision affects thousands of containers per vessel – with the consequences of any misstep felt throughout the supply chain.
The company’s proactive approach to fleetwide digitalisation has therefore been devised with one overarching objective in mind: to simplify its operations.

Operations are expected to commence in the fourth quarter of 2027. The awards build on ADNOC Drilling’s experience in offshore operations and support the regional expansion pillar of Drill-to-Operate, which identifies strategic partnerships and access to new customers, markets and revenue streams as important drivers of long-term growth. The contracts are expected to make their first full-year financial contribution in 2028, with the expected 2027 contribution already reflected in the preliminary 2027 guidance previously communicated. The awards remain subject to applicable conditions and completion of the relevant contractual formalities.
