articles.title: “Welcome to a Dying Industry”: Inside Rik van Hemmen’s Maritime Journey
articles.summary: From a Dutch maritime family to America's Cup yacht design and the president of Martin & Ottaway, a 150-year-old engineering firm, Rik van Hemmen has walked a unique path through the maritime industry. van Hemmen recently visited with Maritime Matters: The MarineLink Podcast…
articles.body: “Welcome to a Dying Industry”: Inside Rik van Hemmen’s Maritime Journey Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Greg Trauthwein , Editor Gregory R. Trauthwein has covered the global maritime market for more than 25... November 9, 2026 “If things get strange, we get the call.” Rik van Hemmen standing on the beach in front of the M/V New Carissa, a 639-foot bulk carrier that ran aground on the Oregon coast near Coos Bay in 1999. Image courtesy Rik van Hemmen The M/V New Carissa, a 639-foot bulk carrier that ran aground on the Oregon coast near Coos Bay in 1999. Image courtesy Rik van Hemmen The M/V New Carissa, a 639-foot bulk carrier that ran aground on the Oregon coast near Coos Bay in 1999. Image courtesy Rik van Hemmen The M/V New Carissa, a 639-foot bulk carrier that ran aground on the Oregon coast near Coos Bay in 1999. Image courtesy Rik van Hemmen The formative years of Rik's maritime career! Image courtesy Rik van Hemmen Rik van Hemmen today. Francis Sprague Martin, in 1875 the founder of what would become Martin & Ottaway; an inspirtation for the company's book "Let Me Be Frank", which celebrates the organizations 150 year anniversary. Photo courtesy Rik van Hemmen From a Dutch maritime family to America's Cup yacht design and the president of Martin & Ottaway, a 150-year-old engineering firm, Rik van Hemmen has walked a unique path through the maritime industry. van Hemmen recently visited with Maritime Matters: The MarineLink Podcast, to share his views on everything from maritime engineering, technology, fuel, education and the future of shipping. In 1988, a 28-year-old Rik van Hemmen attended a cocktail party at the Four Seasons in New York City, surrounded by senior shipping executives and shipowners. He had recently joined Martin & Ottaway, the maritime engineering and consulting company where his father, Hank van Hemmen, was a partner. One of the industry veterans offered the young engineer a greeting he has never forgotten. “Welcome to a dying industry.” Van Hemmen, never particularly inclined to accept conventional wisdom, had an answer. “Yeah, but all you guys are old and you're going to be dead soon and then it will be all mine, or whatever is left.” Nearly four decades later, the president of Martin & Ottaway can appreciate the humor in that exchange. The older generation has largely passed, but the maritime industry has done anything but disappear. “The truth of it is that this industry didn't go away. It's just different,” said van Hemmen. While American deepsea shipping has unquestionably declined, maritime commerce has expanded, technology has advanced and the definition of what constitutes the maritime industry has grown considerably. “I'm still a small player in a big industry,” he said. “Today, the technology and the engineering is much more interesting than it was back in the 80s.” That perspective is informed by a career that has taken him through defense engineering, classification, America's Cup yacht design, marine casualties, technology development and the management of one of the industry's oldest engineering consultancies. It also comes from a family history that explains why van Hemmen approaches maritime engineering as something considerably larger than designing ships. Courtesy Rik van Hemmen “I'm a son of a son of a sailor” Van Hemmen was born in the Netherlands in 1960, into a family in which maritime engineering was an established profession. His father and grandfather were ship engineers, although neither began his career as a business owner. Maritime was part of everyday life. As a schoolboy, he brought photos of enormous Dutch tugboats to show and tell. His father's work provided opportunities to visit ships and waterfront facilities. But on particularly acute memory has little to do with ships themselves. As a six-year-old, van Hemmen sat in the Lotus Formula One car driven by Jim Clark, which was being transported by the shipping company employing his father. The experience left a lasting impression, but it did not settle his career ambitions. Born at the beginning of the space age, van Hemmen was fascinated by aerospace engineering. He could readily imagine pursuing something other than maritime. His family's connection to the industry, however, extended back another generation, and the story of how his grandfather entered shipping is revealing. His grandfather, Hendrik Fokko, was the eldest of 12 children. His father was a cigar maker, and the younger Hendrik initially trained as a blacksmith. Seeking better opportunities, he decided to apply to a school for railway engineers. On the tram to the school, an older passenger asked where he was going. When Hendrik explained his plans, the stranger suggested he stay aboard for one more stop and apply to the marine engineering school instead. The money, the stranger explained, was better at sea. He followed the advice and became a ship engineer. For van Hemmen, the story illustrates something important: even in a country with the maritime heritage of the Netherlands, the connection between a young person and a maritime career can be remarkably tenuous, a resounding message today as the industry collectively seeks to attract and retain the next generation. And in fact, van Hemmen’s own route was hardly more direct. The family moved to the United States in 1976 when van Hemmen was 16. Approaching high school graduation, he had made little effort to investigate college until a guidance counselor intervened. Maritime academies were suggested, but van Hemmen was not yet an American citizen and could not attend under the admission rules then in place. He began examining engineering programs and discovered Virginia Tech's aerospace and ocean engineering program. Stevens Institute of Technology was another possibility, particularly because of its involvement in America's Cup research. Virginia Tech ultimately won out. Model Testing @ Virginia Tech in 1981, with hair and proper lab wear ... Virginia Tech T shirt and cut off jeans. Photo by Mark Tesh, van Hemmen's Virginia Tech research partner. Van Hemmen studied aerospace and ocean engineering, a combination reflecting the shifting engineering priorities of the 1970s. With the space program and defense aerospace markets contracting, ocean engineering was being promoted as a new frontier. Deep sea mining, an industry still attempting to establish itself commercially today, was among the emerging opportunities. Financial necessity led van Hemmen into cooperative education, including work for a defense contractor on submarine warfare projects. He also spent time with the American Bureau of Shipping, a well-paying surveyor position in New York. He took the job and bought a sailboat, but the office routine did not suit him. “I just did not like the job. It really made me miserable,” he recalled. On a whim, he applied to work in America's Cup yacht design. He got the job, accepted a substantial pay cut, sailed his boat to Newport and spent four years designing yachts. By 1988, with a wife, child and mortgage, the economics of yacht design had become less appealing. Harry Ottaway, his father's business partner, suggested bringing him into Martin & Ottaway. His father agreed, with one condition. “You don't work for me, you're going to work for Harry Ottaway.” Van Hemmen joined the company that year, beginning a professional association that continues today. Rik van Hemmen -- young yacht designer. “If things get strange, we get the call” Martin & Ottaway recently celebrated its 150th anniversary, an occasion marked by the publication of Let Me Be Frank: Martin & Ottaway, 150 Years. The title refers partly to three generations of company leadership named Francis Martin. It also reflects the book's approach to recounting the company's history, with the founding Francis Martin serving as a narrative voice, even beyond his death in 1921. For van Hemmen, the title has a third meaning: an attempt to speak candidly about the maritime business. That candor is evident in how he describes the firm. “We're an engineering company that really is involved in wide ranging problem solving,” he said. “We don't just use calculations and drafting and stuff like that to solve the problem. We go deep into the maritime adventure in solving the problem.” The company works across engineering, insurance, legal disputes, finance, cargo operations and maritime economics. Its engineers are frequently brought into situations where something has failed, whether a vessel, a technology, a commercial arrangement or an operating procedure. “The vast majority of problems that we have are failures,” he said. With approximately 10 engineers, the company handles about 200 projects annually. Van Hemmen estimates its client base at 600 to 700, although some clients may call only once in 20 years. “They generally know that if things gets strange and complicated, we get a call.” Maritime's Greatest Problem? Getting People in the Door Ask van Hemmen about the industry's workforce shortage and the conversation quickly moves beyond wages, recruitment campaigns and maritime academies. His concern is more fundamental. “The problem we have today is the general public doesn't know how to enter it. It's too isolated.” Historically, maritime careers were visible. Ships lined working waterfronts, and young people could encounter the industry simply by walking down a pier. Today's waterfronts are often recreational spaces, separated from the commercial operations that sustain the economy. Someone watching a containership enter New York Harbor might be fascinated by the vessel, but have no idea how to turn that interest into a career. Van Hemmen wants to change that through SL7 Expo, an initiative proposing to convert a former SL7 containership, subsequently converted into a roll-on/roll-off vessel, into a major maritime exhibition and education center. Make no mistake: the concept is not simply a museum of maritime history, rather it would emphasize contemporary careers, technology and opportunities, connecting visitors with the industry's many routes to employment. Van Hemmen envisions an attraction comparable in ambition to the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum, complemented by practical waterfront programs. The organizers submitted an unsolicited proposal to MARAD, but van Hemmen said the agency declined to support it on cost grounds. He cited an estimated $20 million annual requirement associated with maintaining the ship. His frustration is rooted in the contrast between spending on maritime infrastructure and the limited resources devoted to introducing people to the industry. “Maritime is a human enterprise,” he said. “If you don't bring the humans in, you can spend all the money you want. It's just not going to happen.” He believes the industry should particularly reach communities where maritime careers are not traditionally considered. The opportunity is not simply to fill shipboard positions. It is to provide a route into skilled employment and the middle class. But van Hemmen's argument goes further. He believes maritime experience produces better decision makers, even among people who ultimately pursue other professions. “Maritime is one of the best training grounds in the world for humans,” said van Hemmen, citing its combination of independence, teamwork, responsibility and manageable risk makes. “You need to put the kids in the real to make them powerful.” Young people need opportunities to make mistakes, learn from them and develop confidence. They also need mentors willing to admit they do not always have the answers. “The best teachers say, ‘I have no idea. Let's figure it out together.’” Fuel: The Path Ahead When talk turns to maritime tech, Van Hemmen believes the adoption of heavy fuel oil ranks prominently. He argues that the industry's decision to place relatively unprocessed residual fuel aboard ships and require crews to clean it through onboard treatment systems represents an example of commercial incentives producing an inefficient overall result. His daughter, who previously worked at Martin & Ottaway and now works for Ørsted, once questioned why the fuel was not cleaned to a consistent standard before delivery. He agreed. “This is a classic case of a failure where economically something gets done, but when you look at the actual result of it, it's just plain stupid.” He is not arguing that heavy fuel oil could never have been used. His objection concerns how the system evolved and where the operational burden was placed. By contrast, he regards the International Maritime Organization as an example of successful international cooperation. He credits IMO with helping establish broadly accepted rules that improved maritime safety and environmental performance, citing MARPOL and double hull tanker requirements. “People like to make fun of United Nations, but IMO is part of United Nations. If you want to talk about success, it's incredible.” His larger frustration concerns the absence of consistent strategic direction, particularly in government programs. Recalling his defense engineering experience, van Hemmen describes promising technical projects that were abruptly canceled, leaving engineers to pack away their work. He sees a similar lack of sustained direction contributing to problems in U.S. Navy shipbuilding. “A government needs to set goals and let commerce achieve the goals and the winner makes money.” Without clear objectives, he argues, even capable engineers and shipbuilders struggle to deliver economical results. A Hybrid Future Van Hemmen sees the transition to cleaner marine energy as one of the industry's most important coming decisions. He expects hybrid propulsion arrangements to become increasingly common, with designers balancing batteries, engines and fuel choices according to vessel requirements. But he also believes shipping would benefit from convergence around a broadly usable fuel. His current preference is methanol. “I think methanol is the way to go.” He favors its handling and distribution characteristics, its potential use in combustion engines and fuel cells, and the relative ease of integrating it into existing fuel supply practices. He is careful to distinguish a preference from a definitive prediction. “I'm not saying that is the actual answer, and I'm actually in a study group that is trying to figure out if I'm stupid or not.” He previously believed liquid hydrogen would emerge as a broadly transportable fuel and acknowledges that his thinking has changed. Hydrogen, he believes, will remain important, particularly as a means of converting surplus renewable energy into other fuels. His principal concern is that shipowners may select fuels based on immediate price advantages without fully considering long-term operating and infrastructure consequences. Ammonia is one example. Van Hemmen worries that its potential economic advantages could encourage widespread adoption before the industry fully accounts for its toxicity and handling requirements. The result, he fears, could resemble the historical experience with heavy fuel oil. Autonomy & Maintenance Van Hemmen expects autonomous technology to become an increasingly important part of maritime operations. He is less convinced that large oceangoing cargo ships will soon operate entirely without crews, as machinery requires maintenance during a voyage. “It makes much more sense to have maintenance on these ships with crews that maintain them as the ship is running than to do it on the dock.” He expects automation to reduce certain watchkeeping requirements and shift some navigation and planning functions ashore. But removing every person from a large commercial vessel creates operational and economic problems that cannot be solved through navigation software alone. “So you probably have fewer watchstanders, you have reduced bridge crew, maybe navigational planning takes place ashore, stuff like that. But to see truly unmanned ships going, I don't quite see that yet.” He approaches artificial intelligence with similar pragmatism. Martin & Ottaway is actively experimenting with AI for research, engineering calculations and maintenance planning. Van Hemmen describes using AI to calculate vessel deceleration in a marine casualty investigation. The system quickly produced the relevant equations and a useful technical explanation. But he emphasizes the need for professional judgment. “A lot of times it's not,” he said of AI-generated answers. “So that judgment still has to be there anyway.” AI can shorten the route to an answer. It does not eliminate the engineer's responsibility to determine whether the answer is correct. Solar Hybrid Electric Wheelchair Accessible Catamaran (SHEWAC) Aberration: After his wife became wheelchair bound, van Hemmen designed and had built a 35-foot hybrid propulsion wheelchair friendly catamaran. Together with the boat design and construction masters of Scarano boats, he converted a 1996 medium to high performance 35-foot sailing catamaran . Image courtesy Rik van Hemmen Click Here here for full insights on the SHEWAC The Next 150 Years For all his interest in emerging technology, van Hemmen returns repeatedly to people. His father and grandfather remain his most important influences. Both, he recalls, were accomplished technical managers who gave younger colleagues the confidence to work independently. When those colleagues encountered problems, the response was not criticism. It was an invitation to solve the problem together. Other mentors included yacht designer Johan Valentijn and engineers who helped develop his technical expertise. Van Hemmen also draws inspiration from people outside maritime, including Admiral Wayne Meyer, Ted Turner, Pete Seeger, John Lewis and others who demonstrated independence, leadership or a willingness to challenge convention. At Martin & Ottaway, he has tried to create a culture in which engineers with different backgrounds and viewpoints work together. His most important management lesson is straightforward. “Don't hire somebody like yourself.” For a consulting firm regularly called upon to solve unusual problems, intellectual diversity is a practical necessity. “If everybody speaks the same tune, then you're going to get tunnel vision. And we fight tunnel vision every day.” His advice to someone considering maritime is to develop genuine expertise, demonstrate initiative and become comfortable working through unfamiliar problems. The industry, after all, is not short of challenges. And if van Hemmen's career demonstrates anything, it is that a maritime career rarely follows a predictable course. Nearly 40 years after being welcomed to a supposedly dying industry, he sees more opportunities, more complicated technology and more reasons for young people to become involved. The task now is to make sure they know those opportunities exist. The Martin & Ottaway Crew today. articles.body: Gulftainer has launched a new bonded logistics corridor connecting Fujairah Terminal with Sharjah Dry Ports in Sajaa, United Arab Emirates, expanding inland cargo movement options between the two locations. The service allows customers to move cargo under customs bond from Fujairah to Sharjah, where customs clearance can take place. It is designed to simplify cargo handling and provide an alternative route for shipments entering the UAE. According to Gulftainer, the new corridor includes an offer of 12 days of free storage. The company has not specified whether the offer applies to all cargo categories or is subject to additional conditions. Strengthening inland logistics connectivity The new connection links Fujairah’s maritime facilities with the inland logistics infrastructure at Sharjah Dry Ports, allowing cargo to move between the two locations under customs control. Customers can arrange customs clearance in Sharjah rather than completing the process at the initial port of arrival. This provides an additional option for companies managing cargo distribution within the UAE. The launch builds on Gulftainer’s earlier investment in inland logistics infrastructure, including the development of bonded dry port facilities in Sajaa . Gulftainer has also recently introduced the Sharjah Dry Ports name for its Sajaa operations, reflecting the facility’s role in the company’s wider logistics network. The company has not disclosed the expected cargo volumes, frequency of movements or transit times for the new Fujairah–Sharjah corridor. The service adds another inland transport option to Gulftainer’s UAE logistics operations, combining port connectivity with customs-controlled cargo movements and storage services.

articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard is concluding its scheduled 2026 seasonal evaluation of six Saildrone Voyager Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) on the Great Lakes this week ahead of forecasted winter icing conditions. Following the completion of this seasonal evaluation…
articles.body: Coast Guard Wraps Up Seasonal Great Lakes USV Evaluation Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 9, 2026 Credit: Adobe Stock/Selene Miller The U.S. Coast Guard is concluding its scheduled 2026 seasonal evaluation of six Saildrone Voyager Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) on the Great Lakes this week ahead of forecasted winter icing conditions. Following the completion of this seasonal evaluation, the Coast Guard intends to conduct an additional test and evaluation period in the spring of 2027 as part of a service-wide effort to evaluate how autonomous technologies enhance Coast Guard missions and assist operators. Deployed between April and November 2026 across the Great Lakes, the six 33-foot, wind- and solar-powered vessels provided Coast Guard command centers and boat stations with real-time offshore weather data and operational insight across thousands of square miles of open water. Rather than replacing Coast Guard personnel, autonomous surface vessels act as force multipliers that assist in Coast Guard mission execution so cutters, boats, and aircraft can focus on high-priority lifesaving and law enforcement missions: - Real-Time Weather and Wave Forecasting for Search and Rescue: Weather on the Great Lakes can turn dangerous in minutes. By measuring wind speed, wave height, water temperature, and barometric pressure out on open water, these floating sensors tell Coast Guard rescue crews what conditions a stranded boater or capsized kayaker is facing before a rescue boat even leaves the pier. - Spotting Emergencies Faster Across 94,000 Square Miles: Understanding normal seasonal boating and commercial shipping traffic on the Great Lakes helps Coast Guard watchstanders immediately identify when something is out of place—such as a disabled vessel drifting toward shoals, a navigation hazard, or unsafe activity after dark. - Protecting Local Fisheries: Maintaining visibility along the international maritime boundary line helps fisheries enforcement officers ensure commercial fishing vessels remain on their respective side of the border, protecting local sportsmen, charter captains, and domestic fisheries. - Helping Human Crews Work Smarter Alongside Canadian Partners: Instead of resourcing a Coast Guard boat and crew to observe open water or check weather conditions miles offshore, a wind-powered sensor sailboat handles routine observation so Coast Guard men and women are ready to launch the moment someone calls for help. Each 33-foot Saildrone Voyager is propelled by the wind with an auxiliary 4 kW electric motor and is equipped with marine radar, an Automatic Identification System (AIS) transceiver, meteorological instruments, and an optical camera. To guarantee safe navigation around recreational and commercial vessels, every USV is remotely piloted 24/7 by human operators in mission control centers distributed across three time zones. This Great Lakes deployment builds upon previous Coast Guard autonomous evaluations in the Southeast, Southwest, and Northeast districts, as well as historic capital investments to modernize the Service's fleet and technology. By testing autonomous systems across various geographic environments, the Coast Guard ensures its operating force remains agile, capable, and responsive to evolving mission demands.

File Photo: Alexandre Tziripouloff/Shutterstock France on Monday laurched a new G7-backed network linking major seaports, customs authorities and international organizations in an effort to crack down on drug trafficking through global maritime supply chains. The G7+ Ports Network to Combat Drug Trafficking, announced during the G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris on November 9, brings together 14 ports and participating countries, including Brazil and South Korea, alongside the G7 nations. The initiative aims to improve intelligence sharing, strengthen cooperation between port and customs authorities, and better identify shipping routes and containers being exploited by criminal organizations. The network was first proposed at the G7 leaders’ summit in Évian, France, in June, when leaders issued a joint declaration identifying maritime transport as the primary route for international drug and precursor chemical trafficking. The declaration committed participating countries to strengthening maritime security, improving port resilience and working more closely with the shipping industry to disrupt illicit cargo movements. The new network will coordinate with existing initiatives, including the European Ports Alliance, and draw on international standards such as the International Maritime Organization’s International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code. Its work will include sharing best practices, improving cooperation between law enforcement agencies and port operators, and identifying vulnerabilities in international cargo supply chains. The initiative also involves organizations including the IMO, Interpol, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the World Customs Organization. According to France’s Foreign Ministry , the network is holding its first meeting in Marseille alongside the November 9–10 G7 ministerial gathering in Paris. The effort comes amid growing concerns over the infiltration of legitimate port operations and logistics networks by organized criminal groups. In their June declaration, G7 leaders warned that criminal organizations increasingly rely on access to legitimate public and private institutions to facilitate international drug shipments. They also called for stronger cooperation with the private sector and improvements to port and shipping security standards. France has made maritime trafficking a central part of its broader international counternarcotics strategy. In a new action plan released Monday , the government estimated that 70% of drugs entering Europe arrive by sea and through ports. The French government said it handled 20 requests to board vessels suspected of drug trafficking on the high seas in 2025, resulting in seizures of nearly 40 metric tons of narcotics, almost entirely cocaine. The G7 initiative also calls for stronger efforts to prevent criminal infiltration of port authorities and private businesses, alongside enhanced financial investigations targeting the proceeds of drug trafficking. For the maritime industry, the initiative places additional attention on the security of commercial ports, containerized cargo and international logistics operations, with governments seeking closer cooperation from shipping companies and terminal operators. The challenge now will be turning the new network into practical cooperation between ports and enforcement agencies while protecting the flow of legitimate international trade. November 9, 2026 © Adobe Stock/namning Gulf bourses closed mostly higher on Monday as US President Donald Trump's signal that fresh Iran strikes are unlikely, provided talks continue, lifted sentiment across the region after an eight-month conflict. Trump's remarks came despite reports from the US military and Iranian state media that shipping had been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried nearly a fifth of the world's crude before the war. Trump had earlier hinted at renewed attacks after last week's midterm elections, but no large-scale US military operation has followed, and Tehran has warned it would hit US and Israeli targets in response to any such move. Saudi Arabia's benchmark index rose 0.9%, with Al Rajhi Bank gaining 1.9%, while Perfect Presentation For Commercial Services surged 4.3% following a rise in quarterly profit. Meanwhile, Saudi authorities lifted an alert in Riyadh on Monday, a day after a Houthi attack damaged an Aramco office building in the city. Dubai's main share index gained 1%, with blue-chip developer Emaar Properties advancing 2.4%. In Abu Dhabi, the index was up 1%. Shipping disruption in the Strait of Hormuz remains a drag, but resilient regional economic data is keeping investors buying, said Daniel Takieddine, Co-founder and CEO, Sky Links Capital Group. Anwar Gargash, a senior Emirati official, warned on Monday that the region may face a long period of instability as a comprehensive political deal between Washington and Tehran looked hard to achieve. "We should ... prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted," Gargash said in an address to a geopolitical conference in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates capital. However, Abu Qir Fertilizers fell 2.7%, and Misr Fertilizers Production slid 2.6%, extending the previous session's losses. Egypt has notified fertilizer producers of a further 33% cut to their gas supplies, according to a statement from Abu Qir and industry officials. The move reflects Cairo's push to reduce reliance on costly LNG imports, a shift that hits producers hard because gas is both their raw material and their fuel. articles.title: Fourteen Migrants Die Attempting to Reach Crete by Boat
articles.summary: Fourteen migrants died in an attempt to reach the island of Crete by boat, Greece's coastguard said on Monday, in the second deadly incident in the area in recent days.A Morocco-flagged container ship spotted their boat on Monday about 15 nautical miles (28 km) off the port of Kaloi Limenes.
articles.body: Fourteen Migrants Die Attempting to Reach Crete by Boat Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 9, 2026 © Adobe Stock/lesniewski Fourteen migrants died in an attempt to reach the island of Crete by boat, Greece's coastguard said on Monday, in the second deadly incident in the area in recent days. A Morocco-flagged container ship spotted their boat on Monday about 15 nautical miles (28 km) off the port of Kaloi Limenes. Thirteen migrants were found dead and another died later in hospital, the coastguard said. Eighteen people survived. It was not immediately clear what had caused the deaths. Greek authorities said the boat may have been at sea for days, struggling to reach the shore due to strong winds. "We found them (the survivors) shivering from the cold," said a local coastguard official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. The incident comes after another on Saturday off Crete in which the coastguard retrieved eight bodies and rescued 28 migrants from Sudan, the coastguard said. In three other incidents on Monday, the coast guard rescued another 187 migrants. On Monday, a Reuters photo showed a body wrapped in a black bag being taken ashore at the port of Agia Galini. Four of the survivors were taken to hospital on Monday, including a toddler. The other survivors were taken to a migrant facility on Crete, the coastguard said. Greece, long a favoured gateway to Europe for migrants and refugees from the Middle East, Africa and Asia, was on the front line of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-2016 when nearly 1 million people landed on its islands, mainly from Turkey. Total migrant arrivals have since ebbed as Athens has bolstered sea and border patrols. But arrivals from Libya of migrants — mostly fleeing violence in Sudan and Bangladesh — have surged in recent years. (Reuters)

articles.body: Salvage teams have removed approximately 84% of the MSC Baltic III wreck from Cedar Cove in Newfoundland and Labrador, according to the Canadian Coast Guard. Resolve Marine has removed 9,282 tonnes from the grounded container vessel as dismantling work enters its final stages. The vessel’s bow section has been brought fully ashore, dismantled and removed from the beach. This phase included the removal of six priority heavy fuel oil tanks. Intermittent oil sheening continues to be observed in Cedar Cove. However, the Canadian Coast Guard said the sheening has decreased significantly since the bow section was removed from the water. Final stern sections remain in the water One section of the vessel’s stern has also been pulled ashore, dismantled and removed from the shoreline. The salvage contractor is now preparing pulling operations for the two remaining stern sections still in the water. The Canadian Coast Guard and Environment and Climate Change Canada continue to monitor the area for pollution. Surveillance includes shoreline inspections and observations from the water and air, subject to weather conditions. MSC Baltic III grounded in Cedar Cove near Lark Harbour on 15 February 2025 after losing power during severe weather. All 20 crew members were rescued safely. The 2,478 TEU container vessel was carrying approximately 400 containers when it grounded. Cargo and pollutants were removed before the wreck was dismantled progressively and pulled ashore in sections.

REUTERS/Mohammed Aty The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is calling for stronger protections for merchant ships and their crews as continued attacks in the Middle East, Red Sea and Black Sea put seafarers at risk and threaten vital shipping routes. The warning follows the IMO Council’s 138th session in London last week, where members addressed a growing list of maritime security threats, including the war involving Iran, Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and Russian strikes on shipping and port infrastructure in Ukraine. According to the IMO’s latest figures, at least 130 incidents involving commercial vessels have been confirmed in the Middle East since the conflict began, with 25 seafarers now reported killed. The latest fatality occurred aboard the tanker Velos Sapphire, which was attacked last week. Thousands of other seafarers remain at risk, including crews aboard vessels unable to leave the Persian Gulf. “Seafarers continue to lose their lives, suffer serious injuries, face abandonment, are denied repatriation and are deprived of basic human necessities, including water, food and medical care, resulting from the ongoing geopolitical conflicts,” IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said. The Council reiterated that international shipping lanes must remain open, safe and secure, stressing that seafarers should not bear the consequences of geopolitical disputes beyond their control. It also urged member states to refrain from unlawful actions that could endanger commercial shipping and called for additional measures to prevent further loss of life. Dominguez pledged to examine what more the IMO can do to protect crews and ease the humanitarian consequences of the ongoing conflicts. The concerns extend well beyond the Strait of Hormuz. The Council strongly condemned Houthi attacks against merchant vessels and crews in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait, as well as Russian attacks targeting commercial ships, seafarers, ports and maritime safety infrastructure supporting Ukraine’s Black Sea shipping corridor. It also raised concerns about renewed piracy and armed robbery in the Western Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden, where 17 attempted or actual incidents have been reported since the beginning of 2026. The Council directed Dominguez to continue monitoring developments across these regions and keep member states informed. The maritime security discussions came as the Council also backed Dominguez for a second four-year term, which would extend his leadership through December 2031. The decision remains subject to approval by the IMO Assembly in 2027. Among other decisions, the Council approved an initial £2 million in funding to modernize the IMO’s Global Integrated Shipping Information System and develop an e-learning platform. The Council also selected China’s Yu Jiajia as the recipient of the 2027 IMO Gender Equality Award. The meeting’s conclusions underscore the growing challenge facing the UN maritime agency as attacks on commercial shipping continue across several regions, leaving seafarers exposed to conflicts in which they have little say. articles.summary: U.S. container imports reached their highest level of the year in September, capping an unusually long peak shipping season that has kept major ports busy since the spring despite tariffs,...

Photo courtesy Port of Los Angeles U.S. container imports reached their highest level of the year in September, capping an unusually long peak shipping season that has kept major ports busy since the spring despite tariffs, inflation and growing pressure on supply chains. Ports covered by the National Retail Federation (NRF) and Hackett Associates’ Global Port Tracker handled 2.37 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) of loaded imports in September, up 12.6% from a year earlier and 3.4% from August. The total made September the third-busiest month since Global Port Tracker began keeping records, trailing only July 2025’s 2.39 million TEUs and May 2022’s 2.4 million TEUs. The latest figures also show just how much this year’s import season has defied expectations. As gCaptain reported last month, NRF had expected August to mark the year’s peak, with September volumes projected to decline slightly to 2.28 million TEUs. Instead, September came in roughly 90,000 TEUs above that forecast. “U.S. ports have seen high volume levels throughout this year’s longer-than-usual peak season and numbers are still strong even as the season winds down,” said Jonathan Gold, NRF vice president for supply chain and customs policy. The sustained volumes have not come without problems. Gold said some ports, particularly on the West Coast, have experienced backups as containers wait to be transferred to rail. Labor uncertainty has also emerged at the nation’s busiest container port complex. The International Longshore and Warehouse Union’s Local 26, which represents roughly 250 watchmen at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, has been negotiating a new contract with the Pacific Maritime Association. The two sides extended their existing agreement through November 20 on Friday, averting an immediate strike but leaving the longer-term dispute unresolved. Despite those challenges, Gold said retailers are well positioned for the holiday shopping season, with most seasonal merchandise already in the country. The extended peak season has been driven in large part by changing U.S. tariff policies, which have repeatedly prompted retailers to adjust the timing of their shipments. Hackett Associates founder Ben Hackett said the import surge that began in 2025 appeared to be winding down earlier this year after the Supreme Court struck down the Trump administration’s sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs. But new tariffs introduced during the second quarter triggered another wave of imports beginning in May, which continued through mid-October. “Consumer spending supported this influx, with households continuing to buy despite rising inflation,” Hackett said. With the peak season now winding down, Global Port Tracker expects imports to decline through the final months of 2026, although volumes are still projected to remain above year-earlier levels. October imports are estimated at 2.26 million TEUs, up 9.1% from a year earlier. November is forecast at 2.05 million TEUs, up 1.2%, followed by 2.03 million TEUs in December, up 1.3%. For the full year, imports are now expected to reach 26 million TEUs, a 2% increase over 2025’s 25.4 million TEUs. That represents another upward revision from NRF’s October forecast, which projected 25.8 million TEUs for the year. The outlook points to a slower start in 2027. January imports are forecast at 2.04 million TEUs, down 3% year over year, followed by 1.89 million TEUs in February, down 0.5%, and 1.92 million TEUs in March, down 11.2%. Global Port Tracker tracks loaded container imports at major U.S. ports on the East, West and Gulf coasts, including Los Angeles, Long Beach, New York/New Jersey, Savannah and Houston. articles.summary: Every year, the President’s budget proposes investments in infrastructure projects across the country. For navigation projects on America’s inland waterways, one of the most important factors influencing whether a lock and dam modernization…
articles.body: Looking Beyond the Benefit-to-Cost Ratio: Why America’s Inland Waterways Deserve a Broader Measure of Value Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. By Jen Armstrong, Waterways Council, Inc. Vice President, Government Relations November 9, 2026 Copyright Randy Runtsch/AdobeStock Every year, the President’s budget proposes investments in infrastructure projects across the country. For navigation projects on America’s inland waterways, one of the most important factors influencing whether a lock and dam modernization project advances in the annual budget process is its benefit-to-cost ratio (BCR). On its surface, the concept sounds simple and sensible. A project’s benefits should exceed its costs. The higher the ratio, the stronger the justification for federal investment. But when it comes to inland waterways infrastructure, the formula used by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers captures only a fraction of the value these projects provide to the Nation. As a result, some projects that are critically important to the economy, national security, and energy supply may appear less beneficial on paper than they truly are in practice. What is a Benefit-to-Cost Ratio? The Corps calculates a BCR by comparing the expected economic benefits of a project to the cost of constructing it. For inland navigation projects, the quantified benefits are limited to cost savings- an estimate of how much money shippers will save by moving freight by barge versus another mode of transportation like truck or rail which automatically assumes there is capacity to accommodate the volumes currently transported by barge. The inland waterways system moves hundreds of millions of tons of cargo annually, including grain, fertilizer, coal, petroleum products, aggregates, chemicals, and other bulk commodities. Even small improvements in efficiency can generate significant economic benefits. The problem is not what the BCR measures; the problem is what it does not measure. A System Providing Far More Than Transportation Savings America’s inland waterways network is much more than a freight transportation system. It is a foundational piece of national infrastructure that supports numerous public benefits extending well beyond shipper cost savings. Locks and dams help maintain a reliable navigation channel that enables U.S. agricultural exports to reach global markets competitively. A disruption at a major lock can ripple through supply chains, increase transportation costs, and weaken the international competitiveness of American farmers and manufacturers. The system is also essential to energy security. Inland waterways transport vast quantities of petroleum products, coal, chemicals, and components used throughout the Nation’s energy sector. Maintaining reliable movement of these commodities helps ensure affordable and dependable energy supplies for homes, businesses, and industries. Moreover, inland waterways provide critical resilience and redundancy during disruptions to other transportation networks. When highways become congested, rail service is constrained, or national disasters affect transportation infrastructure, the option rivers provide is even more crucial. Yet these broader economic and strategic benefits generally do not appear in traditional navigation BCR calculations. The National Security Dimension Perhaps the most significant omission is national security. The Department of Defense [War] and the Nation’s industrial base depends on reliable transportation networks capable of moving large volumes of critical materials. America’s waterways support shipyards, energy facilities, steel production, agricultural output, and manufacturing operations that contribute directly or indirectly to national defense readiness. The inland waterways system itself can be viewed as strategic infrastructure. Just as the Nation invests in highways, ports, airports, and military facilities because they serve broader national objectives, locks and dams support capabilities that may become especially important during emergencies or conflicts. A lock modernization project may not generate enough transportation cost savings alone to produce a particularly high BCR. However, if that same project strengthens supply chain resilience, supports defense-related industries, and provides transportation redundancy during crises, its actual value to the Nation is substantially greater than the ratio suggests. Global Competitiveness Matters The United States competes in a global market where transportation efficiency directly affects economic success. Many of America’s major trading competitors continue investing heavily in transportation infrastructure to lower logistics costs and improve export performance. Aging inland waterways infrastructure places the United States at a disadvantage when breakdowns and delays increase transportation costs for domestic producers. The average age of many locks on the inland waterways system exceeds their original design life and unexpected outages become increasingly likely as infrastructure ages. When key locks fail, the consequences extend far beyond local communities. Exporters lose reliability, manufacturers face higher costs, and international customers may seek alternative suppliers. These impacts affect national economic competitiveness, but they are not fully reflected in traditional project economics. Toward a More Comprehensive Evaluation Framework None of this suggests that benefit-to-cost analysis should be abandoned. Fiscal discipline and economic accountability remain essential for responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars. However, major infrastructure investments should be evaluated using a framework that recognizes both economic efficiency and strategic national interests. America’s inland waterways are one of the Nation’s greatest competitive advantages. They move freight safely, efficiently, and with lower emissions than most transportation alternatives. More importantly, they support food security, energy security, economic growth, military readiness, and the resilience of domestic supply chains. If decision makers continue focusing solely on what can be easily measured, they risk undervaluing infrastructure that is vital to the Nation’s future.

articles.summary: Accelerating demand for subsea power and telecoms cable network construction is fuelling major expansion of the world fleet of purpose-designed cable laying, maintenance and repair vessels.Driven by the growth of the offshore renewables sector and its advance into deeper waters…
articles.body: Maritime Market: Cable Layer Fleet Gains Scale, Scope Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. David Tinsley , Contributor David Tinsley has spent all his life in the maritime field... November 9, 2026 Setting a new benchmark in load intake and power setup: Fleeming Jenkin, seen here on trials. Credit: Jan De Nul Nexans Electra sailing from Ulsteinvik in western Norway after delivery, May 2026. Credit: Ulstein High productivity: Nexans Electra has three carousels and the ability to lay four cables simultaneously. Credit: Ulstein Accelerating demand for subsea power and telecoms cable network construction is fuelling major expansion of the world fleet of purpose-designed cable laying, maintenance and repair vessels. Driven by the growth of the offshore renewables sector and its advance into deeper waters, as well as by widening investment in cables connecting electrical grids in different countries, emergent generations of cable ship are distinguished by scale, productivity, and technological intensity. Ongoing geopolitical tensions are also giving a fillip to the development of subsea cable infrastructure, whereby concerns over energy security are being addressed through offshore wind energy and international interconnector projects, further extending the scope for specialized vessels. Belgian international construction and dredging group Jan De Nul is set to take cable ship capacity to a new highpoint with its 215-metre, Chinese-built Fleeming Jenkin. Scheduled for imminent introduction, the vessel brings an unrivalled 28,000-ton cable load intake to the market in a design also distinguished by the capability to operate on methanol fuel. The first of two sisters booked with China Merchants Heavy Industry (CMHI) Haimen yard , the Fleeming Jenkin gives an added edge to competition for assignments in the electrical interconnector and offshore renewable energy sectors. The design’s overall scale facilitates lay jobs in both shallow and ultra-deep waters (down to 4,000 metres) over longer distances with fewer connections and allowing for HVDC cable bundling in a single operation. The ship’s home-grown medium-speed machinery emanates from the Ghent factory of Anglo Belgian Corporation (ABC) . The five main gensets, feeding electrical energy to the propulsion units and maneuvering thrusters, are based on prime movers that will enable firing on methanol, biodiesel or hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) as well as diesel oil. The plant comprises four 12-cylinder DV36MeOH models plus an eight-cylinder DZDMeOH engine, for a maximum combined output of 30,600kW, with emission abatement achieved using SCR and DPF systems. Contributing to the efficiency and designated ultra-low emission vessel (ULEv) concept behind the new breed of cable layer is a hybrid power element featuring a 2.5MWh battery installation and related drive arrangement. The ESS is designed to confer peak shaving, load smoothing, spinning reserve, and optimized engine loading. Second-of-class William Thomson was put into the water in April 2026 and is expected to make her service debut by mid 2027. Meanwhile, a newbuild with a 23,000-tonne capacity for high-voltage (HV) cable is nearing completion in Norway to the account of Danish cable maker group NKT. Developed by Norwegian consultancy Salt Ship Design and due to enter service in 2027, the 177-metre NKT Eleonora will work in conjunction with the 140-metre NKT Victoria to connect offshore wind farms to the onshore grid, as part of a project led by Dutch-German transmission system operator TenneT . Subsea telecoms infrastructure builder OMS Group has two cable layers booked with Ulstein in Norway. (credit: Ulstein) Shipbuilding contractor VARD assigned hull fabrication to its Tulcea yard in Romania, and the vessel was subsequently towed to VARD Brattvaag’s premises in western Norway during July for the final phases of construction and outfitting. The building of the new fleet addition has progressed concurrently with the expansion of HV cable manufacturing facilities at NKT’s Swedish plant at Karlskrona. UK-based Global Marine , a specialist in subsea fiber-optic cable operations, has implemented a fleet development strategy, following-up the mid-2026 purchase of a 128-m Norwegian cable ship with an order for a 100-m newbuild. Nominated shipbuilder Colombo Dockyard has a growing reference list in the sector, and the vessel for Global Marine will be a customized version of a proven type from the portfolio of VARD Design. Conceived primarily to support the British company’s long-term telecoms cable maintenance contracts, while affording more capacity to capitalize on growing demand in the subsea cable market, the new ship will incorporate 1,800-ton of cable storage. She has been engineered with a strong focus on station-keeping capability, reduced energy consumption and resilience. The newbuild will host a hybrid power generating arrangement, melding the four main genset, diesel-electric system with a bank of batteries. Propulsive effect, maneuvering and position-holding precision will be delivered by way of two Azipod electric main propulsion units aft and two tunnel thrusters forward. The construction award to Colombo Dockyard is further testament to the Sri Lankan company’s prowess in penetrating a high-end segment of the international market. References to date include the 113-metre cable layer KDDI Cable Infinity , delivered to her Japanese owner in 2019, and the 100-metre cable layer and repair vessel Sophie Germain, completed in 2023 for Orange Marine of France. Two further newbuilds for the French concern are in hand at Colombo and scheduled to be handed over in March 2028 and January 2029, respectively. The Global Marine ship is expected to follow during the fourth quarter of 2029. The UK firm’s latest acquisition, the 25 year-old Normand Clipper (now CS Clipper), was formalized in June this year pursuant to the end of charter from Solstad Maritime . Encapsulating the VARD VS4125 design, the 128-metre vessel is arranged with two tanks that can hold 5,000t of cable. Malaysian subsea digital infrastructure company the OMS Group has four new cable layers under construction on the strength of ramped-up demand from the telecoms industry. Towards the end of December last, just one week after two newbuilds booked from IHC Offshore Energy were laid down at the Dutch group’s Vietnamese partner yard Pacific Shipbuilding , OMS sealed contracts with Norwegian designer and builder Ulstein for two further cable ships. The respective pairs, while distinct in design, will collectively constitute the Great-class. Danish cable maker NKT has a 23,000-tonne load capacity vessel in build for delivery next year. (credit: NKT). The vessels contracted from the Royal IHC Group are based on its proven Type 22 platform. Each incorporates two cable tanks of an aggregate 6,500-tonne capacity, dual firing lines enabling both lay and maintenance operations, and a plough trenching and cable burial capability to a depth of 3.3 metres. The 128-metre CS Genesis is planned for delivery in 2027, with sistership CS Triumph to follow in 2028. Each of the 130-metre Ulstein duo have also been specified with a maximum intake of 6,500-tonne of fiber optic cable and will employ the proprietary SX252 design featuring the innovative X-Bow configuration for enhanced seakeeping and motion reduction. Highlights of the system delivery from Ulstein Power & Control will be variable speed generator (VSG) technology and banks of batteries. Paris-based Nexans Group strengthened its subsea installation capability this year through the May commissioning of the Norwegian-built cable layer Nexans Electra. Constructed by Ulstein Verft to a Skipsteknisk design, the 150-metre Nexans Electra is a derivative of the technologically acclaimed Nexans Aurora, completed by the same shipbuilder in 2021. The DP3 newbuild, vested with a total cable capacity of 13,500-tonnes on three turntables, furthers the Aurora concept, having the wherewithal to lay up to four cables simultaneously, conducive to large-scale, time-critical schemes. Assigned to Nexans Marine Operations of Oslo, Nexans Electra fulfils new environmental goals through a hybrid power system and five Bergen B33:45L6A-driven main gensets able to run on bio diesel blends. The integrated ABB power and propulsion setup in closed-ring configuration affords high fault tolerance and optimized engine use in DP mode. Italy-headquartered Prysmian Group took delivery in July 2026 of a unique power cable burial tool produced in the UK and destined for utilization on the company’s latest deep-sea cable installation vessels Prysmian Monna Lisa and Prysmian Alessandro Volta. The heavy-duty plough is the first of two contracted from subsea engineering firm SMD in north-east England and provides the wherewithal for electric cable burial at a maximum five metres beneath mean seabed level. A Turkish yard is the cradle for a South Korean cable layer project, overseen by a Norwegian management company with recourse to a Norwegian design house. First steel was cut in June 2026 at Tersan Shipyard’s Yalova premises on LS Marine Solution’s 148-metre newbuild , scheduled for completion during the first half of 2028. Developed by Salt Ship Design , the vessel will provide a capability spanning high-voltage AC, high-voltage DC, and fiber optic cable. Having been responsible for the critical drawing approval stage, OSM Thome is now handling on-site construction supervision. The Korean ship forms part of a supply chain strategy implemented by parent organization LS Cable & Systems , which includes expansion of LS Greenlink , the US submarine cable manufacturing subsidiary on the Chesapeake Bay waterfront in Virginia. Persisting geopolitical instability along with energy transition goals look set to continue to expand the market for building and maintaining subsea infrastructure. REUTERS/Matthew Hatcher The historic SS United States , once the fastest ocean liner in the world, is scheduled to leave Mobile, Alabama, on Monday for its final voyage before being intentionally sunk off Florida’s Gulf Coast later this week. The 990-foot vessel is scheduled to become the world’s largest artificial reef when it is scuttled on Thursday, about 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach, according to Okaloosa County officials. Deployment operations are expected to begin at 10 a.m. local time, weather permitting. The U.S. Coast Guard has established a temporary 100-yard moving safety zone around the vessel and its towing vessels for the transit out of Mobile Bay. The tow is expected to reach the offshore deployment site Tuesday, ahead of Thursday’s planned sinking. The sinking will mark the end of a remarkable maritime career for the ship known as America’s Flagship. Built by Newport News Shipbuilding and delivered in 1952, the SS United States captured the transatlantic speed record on its maiden voyage, crossing the Atlantic in just three days, 10 hours and 40 minutes at an average speed of 35.59 knots. The record still stands. The vessel was retired from service in 1969 and spent nearly three decades laid up in Philadelphia before departing under tow in February 2025. Since arriving in Mobile last March, the ship has undergone extensive environmental remediation in preparation for its new role as an artificial reef. According to county officials, all 128 fuel and lubricant tanks have been emptied and cleaned, all 12 decks have undergone remediation, and hundreds of historic artifacts have been removed for preservation. The vessel’s iconic funnels, radar mast and other components have also been saved for a planned land-based museum. The project has faced a last-minute legal challenge from the SS United States Preservation Foundation, which raised concerns about potential environmental contamination. A federal judge denied an initial emergency request to halt the sinking on Friday, although the group subsequently filed another request. Okaloosa County has said the project remains on schedule. The county expects the wreck to attract divers, recreational fishermen and marine life, while providing a major new tourism attraction along Florida’s Emerald Coast. A public ceremony celebrating the ship’s history is scheduled for Wednesday at the Destin-Fort Walton Beach Convention Center. For Thursday’s sinking, a live viewing party will begin at 9 a.m. at AJ’s Seafood and Oyster Bar in Destin. The deployment will also be livestreamed, with a viewing link to be posted at the official SS United States project website. Officials are preparing for potentially hundreds of spectator vessels near the deployment area and are urging boaters to follow instructions from safety personnel. The artificial reef project was funded through tourism revenues and contributions from project partners. For the SS United States , the planned sinking will close one chapter of American maritime history while beginning another beneath the Gulf. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy: Höegh Autoliners Höegh Autoliners has signed an agreement with Chinese battery manufacturer BYD to install a marine battery system aboard its upcoming Aurora No. 12 car carrier, combining battery storage, solar panels and a shaft generator with ammonia propulsion. The agreement, signed Monday at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, will see the vessel equipped with an integrated energy system designed to reduce fuel consumption and emissions. Scheduled for delivery in May 2028, Aurora No. 12 will be capable of operating on ammonia from the day it leaves the shipyard. Höegh says the ship will be the first deep-sea car carrier to combine all four technologies, making it the most fuel-efficient pure car and truck carrier (PCTC) ever built. “This shows that shipping can take the lead in the green transition. Nobody has done that on a deep-sea car carrier before,” said Höegh Autoliners CEO Andreas Enger. Höegh estimates the combination will reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 1,000 metric tons of CO? equivalent annually while lowering fuel costs. The technology could also help address one of the challenges facing ammonia-powered shipping: the relatively high cost of green ammonia compared with conventional marine fuels. While ammonia produces no CO? when burned, its overall environmental impact depends heavily on how it is produced. “We want to push ourselves technologically and learn what green technology can achieve when it is combined at its best,” said Höegh Autoliners COO Sebjørn Dahl. BYD said the partnership would demonstrate the potential for its containerized battery technology in deep-sea shipping. Aurora No. 12 is part of Höegh Autoliners’ expanding Aurora-class newbuilding program at China Merchants Heavy Industry in China. Each vessel can carry up to 9,100 cars, with the company claiming carbon emissions per vehicle transported can be reduced by as much as 58% compared with conventional car carriers. Options and reserved shipbuilding slots could eventually expand the fleet to 26 vessels. The Aurora-class ships feature engines supplied by Everllence, bridge systems from Kongsberg Maritime and DNV ammonia- and methanol-ready class notations. articles.title: How In-Water Services Are Optimizing Vessel & Infrastructure Repair
articles.summary: For many vessel owners, a problem below the waterline used to mean one answer: get the ship out of the water. This time intensive process consisted of booking a drydock...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network For many vessel owners, a problem below the waterline used to mean one answer: get the ship out of the water. This time intensive process consisted of booking a drydock slot, repositioning the vessel and waiting for a full assessment. In the case of underwater infrastructure, the tooling lacked the technological advances available today and many fixes were complex and time consuming. Now, a growing share of the inspection, maintenance and repair that once required a dry hull can be done in-water by commercial divers. Often it is done faster, at lower cost, and with less risk to the schedule. The list of tasks divers can now handle in-water is more comprehensive than many owners realize. Much of this progress comes down to tooling. Hydraulic and pneumatic tools have transformed what a diver can accomplish in a single shift. Grinders, drills, impact wrenches, bolt tensioners, cutters and hull-cleaning brush carts deliver real torque and precision at depth. Work that once took days of manual effort, or simply could not be done, is now routine. Underwater cutting has advanced in parallel. Oxy-arc and ultra-thermic cutting systems allow divers to sever steel plate, piles and structural members quickly and cleanly. That matters for both repair and removal work, and for emergency response when speed counts. Underwater welding has evolved as well. Wet welding, where the welder-diver works directly in the water with no barrier between the arc and the sea, was once viewed as a temporary fix. Today it is governed by AWS D3.6M, the industry’s underwater welding code. Its Class A welds are intended to perform comparably to surface welds, while Class B covers less critical applications. With qualified procedures and the classification society’s acceptance, some jobs that were once “patch it now, fix it in drydock” can now be permanent. The same advances are reshaping work on the infrastructure vessels depend on. Piers, bulkheads, mooring dolphins, pipelines, bridge foundations and offshore structures all sit in the water, and all need inspecting, maintaining and, eventually, replacing. Commercial divers now handle sophisticated construction and repair these assets in water. They cut and remove piles and pile caps, take down and reinstall mooring dolphins and catwalks, and seal and internally plug pipelines. They drill into the seabed, install piles and foundations, place underwater grout and concrete, and make the subsea connections that allow heavy-lift cranes to set structures in place. Paired with sonar surveys and ROV support, a dive team can assess scour, corrosion and structural damage, then carry out the repair, often in one mobilization. For port authorities, terminal operators and energy companies, that means less downtime for assets that cannot afford to sit idle. If tooling expanded what divers can fix, inspection technology expanded what they can find. And finding the problem early is where most of the value lies. Because high-definition video and still photography are now standard, they quickly produce a clear record for class, insurers and internal review. Non-destructive testing has followed divers into the water. Ultrasonic thickness gauging maps plate wastage across the hull. Other NDT methods help detect cracks and weld defects before they grow into failures. The result is data an engineer can act on, not just a description. Acoustic tools add another layer. Multibeam and side-scan sonar can survey a hull, a berth or a wreck site in poor visibility, where no camera would help. Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) carry cameras and sensors beyond the depth limits of surface-supplied diving, and can monitor diver operations for added safety. The financial case for in-water work starts with what a drydock visit really costs. For a vessel on a tight trading pattern, one unplanned week out of service can cost far more than the repair itself. In-water work addresses each of those costs. A dive team can often mobilize to the vessel’s berth or anchorage. Many jobs can be completed during a scheduled port call, alongside cargo operations, or between voyages. The vessel keeps working, and the schedule holds. Speed of diagnosis matters just as much. When a crew reports vibration, a leak, a loss of thruster performance or suspected grounding damage, the worst outcome is uncertainty. Owners are left choosing between sailing with an unknown problem and pulling the vessel out of service “just in case.” A prompt underwater inspection replaces that guess with facts. Sometimes the answer is a quick in-water fix. Sometimes it confirms that drydock is needed, but now the yard can be booked with a clear scope, the right parts and an accurate estimate. In either scenario, the business interruption is smaller. The capabilities described here are real, but they are not evenly spread across the industry. Owners should stay aware of how far in-water technology has come, and of where any given contractor sits on that curve. Before engaging a vendor, it pays to ask a few direct questions: A contractor with modern tools but thin engineering support, or a long history but outdated methods, may not deliver the speed and certainty owners are paying for. The right partner combines both. Modern tooling, proven underwater welding standards and inspection technology that turns murky water into usable data, and commercial divers can diagnose faster, repair more, and keep vessels operating. For owners, the smartest first call when something goes wrong below the waterline may be to a dive team rather than a shipyard. articles.body: Tidal & Wave Energy November 9, 2026 · 1 minute ago Wavepiston inks new deals in Barbados and Martinique for wave energy NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Wavepiston Danish wave energy firm Wavepiston has signed new deals in Barbados and Martinique related to the development of its projects in these two markets. In Barbados , Wavepiston signed an agreement with the Ministry of Industry, Innovation, Science and Technology (MIST) for the development of its Wave Energy Barbados for Electricity & Water (WEBEW) project, a continuation of collaborative efforts between Wavepiston and the Government of Barbados via Export Barbados (BIDC) , a state-owned enterprise within MIST. Through a phased approach, Wavepiston plans to implement its solution to provide ocean renewable energy and desalinated potable water to the Ocean Valley Data Centre and Industrial Park in St. Andrew. "The project will support the Green Industrial Gateway Advantage (GIGA) Programme and augment Barbados’ and the Latin America & Caribbean (LAC) region’s ambitions for ocean renewable energy. The project will create synergy with the European Union Global Gateway Multi-Country Action Plan supported by CCREEE, EuroClima, UNDP Barbados Eastern Caribbean," Wavepiston said. In Martinique , the Danish firm signed a letter of support with the local government, Collectivité Territoriale de Martinique (CTM), for the 12 MW Wavepiston farm project. According to the company, the first six months of measurements from the wave buoy campaign at its commercial site show slightly higher significant wave heights (Hs) and slightly shorter energy periods (Te) than estimated in the simulated dataset from Copernicus. Using these measured conditions in the performance calculations increases the system’s projected power output by up to 20% compared with estimates based on the Copernicus data. With the support of the Danish Foreign Ministry, Wavepiston reported it was also analyzing the market potential of three additional export markets , with the potential to expand the focus next year. Furthermore, Glosten and Wavepiston have been selected through the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Testing Expertise and Access for Marine Energy Research (TEAMER) program to advance wave energy technology. Glosten will evaluate how the assembly, logistics, and installation of the Wavepiston system can be optimized, with the aim of establishing operational guidelines that support Wavepiston’s next full-scale deployment. articles.summary: Heerema Marine Contractors has extended its global framework agreement with Fugro for another four years. The agreement covers the provision of...
articles.body: News November 9, 2026 · 1 minute ago Heerema renews Fugro deal for offshore survey and positioning services AB Adrijana Buljan Offshore Wind 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Fugro Heerema Marine Contractors has extended its global framework agreement with Fugro for another four years. The agreement covers the provision of survey and positioning support for Heerema’s heavy-lift vessel fleet on offshore installation, decommissioning and offshore wind projects. Under the renewed agreement, Fugro will provide Geo-data, survey and positioning services from January 2027 through December 2030. The work will include support for the transport, installation and removal of offshore structures, including oil & gas platforms and offshore wind foundations. Fugro will also continue using remote operations and other technologies to provide real-time oversight of offshore activities. Its global network of remote operations centers will support offshore project teams with information on vessel and asset positions, movements and installation progress. The extension follows an initial four-year framework agreement signed by the companies in February 2022. That agreement covered survey and positioning services aboard Heerema’s heavy-lift crane vessels, with Fugro deploying technologies including QuickVision, 3Direct and InclinoCam, alongside remote services and specialist teams, according to the Dutch offshore survey specialist. Related Articles Decommissioning Fugro to support Heerema’s offshore installation and decom operations 2 min read The companies have previously worked together on offshore wind installation campaigns, including the 257 MW Arcadis Ost 1 wind farm in Germany , where Fugro’s QuickVision camera technology supported Heerema’s installation of 27 wind turbines using a floating rotor-nacelle assembly method. Fugro said the renewed agreement would create further opportunities to develop technologies and services for increasingly complex offshore campaigns, while supporting operational efficiency, safety and flexibility.
